# Phase 10.2 — Accepted 50-Preset Catalog

Built-in titles use techniques or imagery. Composer names appear only as references/influences, not claims of imitation. Every catalog record must carry the result, performance guidance, references, feature requirements, and an honest availability state.

This catalog is a product brief, not sufficient research evidence. Before a preset becomes operational, three fresh read-only researchers must produce cited historical/primary-source, music-theory, and performer/interaction reports. The parent synthesizes them into stylistic invariants, caricatures to avoid, acceptable approximations, exact configuration, and acceptance examples under `research/NN-slug/`.

**Input default:** clean monophonic notes. Chords are accepted only when a preset says so. Timing-dependent presets require transport.

## Classical — 20

1. **Cloister Organum** — References: Léonin, Pérotin. Result: open fourths, fifths, and octaves around a chant line. Play: slow held stepwise notes with clear phrase rests. Needs: explicit interval stacks.
2. **Modal Linework** — Reference: Palestrina. Result: four smooth modal voices with controlled dissonance. Play: legato scale-shaped melody, moderate pace, few large leaps. Current engine baseline.
3. **Venetian Galleries** — References: Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli. Result: separated choirs answer and combine. Play: short declarations followed by one or two bars of silence. Needs: multiple stable groups and antiphonal routing.
4. **Mensuration Web** — Reference: Ockeghem. Result: one motif at simultaneous proportional speeds. Play: exact three-to-six-note motif with space afterward. Current Free Imitation baseline.
5. **Crabwise Reflection** — Reference: Bach's Crab Canon. Result: a completed phrase returns backward. Play: clean four-to-eight-note phrase, then stop for the reverse answer. Needs: phrase capture and reverse.
6. **Mirror Canon** — References: Bach and Renaissance inversion canons. Result: equal interval inversion around a tonal axis. Play: recognizable angular intervals, no chords. Needs: true axis inversion.
7. **Stretto Engine** — Reference: Bach fugues. Result: tonic, fifth, and octave answers enter progressively closer. Play: repeat a strong two-to-four-note subject with consistent rhythm. Current Strict Canon baseline.
8. **Suspension Garland** — References: Fux, Palestrina. Result: prepared suspensions resolve across strong beats. Play: long legato notes crossing beats and barlines. Current Species IV baseline; transport required.
9. **Ground-Bass Theatre** — References: Monteverdi, Purcell. Result: repeating bass under evolving counterpoint. Play: record a simple bass figure, then a freer upper melody. Needs: recordable ostinato lane.
10. **Alberti Clockwork** — References: Mozart, Clementi. Result: low-high-middle-high accompaniment. Play: sustained melody or simple harmony changes on downbeats. Needs: beat-synchronized pattern lane.
11. **Motive Forge** — Reference: Beethoven. Result: a small motif is fragmented, displaced, and expanded. Play: repeat one emphatic three-to-five-note idea and leave development space. Needs: motif recognition and transforms.
12. **Planed Cathedral** — Reference: Debussy. Result: whole-tone or pentatonic parallel chord planes. Play: slow spacious line, sustained notes, few tonal cadences. Current harmony baseline.
13. **Axis Mirror** — Reference: Bartók. Result: symmetrical reflections around a recurring center. Play: alternate steps and bold leaps around one anchor note. Needs: pitch-class axis mapping.
14. **Color-Mode Windows** — Reference: Messiaen. Result: rotating whole-tone, octatonic, and augmented colors. Play: sparse strongly articulated modal notes. Current symmetric-scale baseline; chord rotations are an extension.
15. **Micropolyphonic Cloud** — Reference: Ligeti. Result: many micro-delayed lines blur into a shifting mass. Play: very few long tones, gentle bends, gradual dynamics. Needs: micro-delays, detune, density, and more bounded voices.
16. **Tintinnabuli Halo** — Reference: Arvo Pärt. Result: a melody is shadowed by nearest tonic-triad tones. Play: slow plain stepwise line with meaningful silence. Needs: tintinnabuli harmony strategy.
17. **Phase Lattice** — Reference: Steve Reich. Result: repeated patterns drift out of phase and realign. Play: repeat an exact three-to-eight-note cell for several bars. Needs: phrase loop and fine time ratios; transport required.
18. **Broken Consort** — Reference: Caroline Shaw. Result: fragments pass, align, and break apart. Play: irregular two-to-five-note gestures separated by breaths. Needs: fragment capture and recombination.
19. **Kinetic Blocks** — Reference: Anna Meredith. Result: accented rhythmic blocks collide with bright repetitions. Play: staccato repeats, octave jumps, and exact accents. Needs: accent patterns and polymeter.
20. **Spectral Bloom** — References: Grisey, Murail, Saariaho. Result: harmony expands from overtone relationships. Play: long expressive notes with velocity, bend, vibrato, and register changes. Needs: partial-derived microtonal voicing.

## Jazz — 15

21. **Sectional Velvet** — Reference: Duke Ellington. Result: low, middle, and high groups act like contrasting sections. Play: lyrical medium-tempo line with dynamics and response space. Needs: arrangement subgroups and articulation.
22. **Stride Engine** — References: James P. Johnson, Fats Waller. Result: alternating bass and chord punches. Play: clear swinging melody or chord tones; do not provide a busy bass. Needs: bass/chord pattern lane.
23. **Sixth-Diminished Conveyor** — Reference: Barry Harris. Result: sixth chords alternate with diminished passing harmony. Play: connected bebop eighths, chromatic approaches, clear resolutions. Current engine baseline.
24. **Angular Cells** — Reference: Thelonious Monk. Result: tritones, clusters, displaced responses, and negative space. Play: short dry motifs with surprising accents and long rests. Needs: bounded clusters and displacement.
25. **Bebop Chase** — References: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie. Result: fast phrases are pursued by shortened delayed answers. Play: clean four-to-eight-note bursts with gaps. Current Free Imitation baseline.
26. **Rootless Glass** — Reference: Bill Evans. Result: smooth rootless ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth voicings. Play: ballad lines, sustained upper tones, gentle chromatic approaches. Needs: extensions, root omission, guide-tone targeting.
27. **Quartal Colossus** — Reference: McCoy Tyner. Result: forceful fourth stacks in Dorian or pentatonic space. Play: assertive modal riffs with rhythmic repetition. Current harmony baseline.
28. **Third-Cycle Labyrinth** — Reference: John Coltrane. Result: tonal centers rotate through major thirds. Play: repeat a compact motif while harmony changes beneath it. Needs: harmonic timeline and key cycle.
29. **Shout Counterpoint** — Reference: Charles Mingus. Result: bass ostinato, gospel response, and unruly counterline. Play: forceful two-bar blues calls followed by a full response opening. Needs: pattern, response, and multiple groups.
30. **Free Quartet** — Reference: Ornette Coleman. Result: independent contours and tonal centers. Play: exploratory lines with wide leaps and pauses to answer the ensemble. Needs: per-lane tonal centers and controlled independence.
31. **Side-Slip Matrix** — Reference: Herbie Hancock. Result: quartal harmony slips a semitone outside and returns. Play: simple inside-key modal motif; let the preset supply outside motion. Needs: timed side-slip timeline.
32. **Harmonic Maze** — Reference: Wayne Shorter. Result: ambiguous movement among diatonic, hexatonic, whole-tone, and octatonic regions. Play: sustained unresolved cells that avoid obvious cadences. Needs: weighted harmonic-state graph.
33. **Metric Labyrinth** — References: Tigran Hamasyan, Vijay Iyer. Result: percussive counterpoint across uneven groupings. Play: repeat an exact accented figure in 5, 7, or grouped 4/4. Needs: odd-meter pattern lanes; transport required.
34. **Chamber Sky** — References: Maria Schneider, Kenny Wheeler. Result: lyrical voices expand into airy ensemble harmony. Play: breath-shaped arcs, wide expressive intervals, soft attacks, long releases. Needs: groups, registers, and gradual entries.
35. **Elastic Counter-Groove** — References: Esperanza Spalding, Brad Mehldau, Robert Glasper. Result: syncopated harmony alternates with contrapuntal answers. Play: concise one- or two-bar riffs with deliberate holes. Needs: groove-aware response detection.

## Video game and interactive — 15

36. **Pixel Trio** — References: early console writing, Koji Kondo, Manami Matsumae. Result: melody, bass, and one counterline obey three-channel economy. Play: compact memorable single-note hooks with clear repeated rhythm. Current engine baseline.
37. **Fractured Crystal** — Reference: Disasterpeace, especially FEZ's constraint-driven linear writing. Result: a tiny motif fractures into limited-voice ostinatos and modal echoes. Play: repeat a three-to-five-note motif slowly, alter one note, and leave substantial air. Needs: bounded motif memory, sparse ostinato, and voice stealing.
38. **Summit Pulse** — Reference: Lena Raine. Result: intimate improvisatory melody grows into rhythmic upper layers. Play: begin softly with hesitant fragments and increase register, velocity, and repetition. Needs: intensity sensing and adaptive scenes.
39. **Adaptive Pilgrim** — References: Austin Wintory, Jessica Curry, Gareth Coker. Result: arrangement follows the emotional intensity arc. Play: isolated sustained notes, then longer/louder phrases, then withdraw. Needs: continuous intensity analysis and scene morphing.
40. **Ash and Ember** — References: Darren Korb, Ashley Barrett. Result: rough modal riffs receive acoustic, metallic, and vocal-like answers. Play: gritty short riffs, strong downbeats, slides, dramatic pauses. Needs: riff-response patterns; sound remains a separate suggestion.
41. **Blocks at Dusk** — Reference: C418. Result: sparse figures accumulate soft extended harmony. Play: two or three gentle notes repeated with small variations and long decay space. Needs: sparse-loop lane and probabilistic entry.
42. **Clockwork Stars** — Reference: Ben Prunty. Result: recurring motifs reappear across registers and counter-rhythms. Play: repeat a clean four-to-eight-note motif while preserving its rhythm. Needs: motif identity and recurrence tracking.
43. **Hollow Choir** — Reference: Christopher Larkin. Result: dark minor melody expands into distant chorale and counterline. Play: singable minor phrases, held destinations, long pauses. Current engine baseline; register groups improve it.
44. **Memory Weave** — Reference: Toby Fox. Result: two learned themes return transformed and combined. Play: teach two clearly distinct motifs, repeating each twice with a pause. Needs: named motif slots and combination.
45. **Neon Noir** — Reference: Shoji Meguro. Result: minor jazz-funk harmony with chromatic passing motion and rhythmic responses. Play: tight syncopated riffs, repeated notes, short chromatic runs. Needs: groove pattern, approaches, bass response.
46. **Forest Layer Unfold** — Reference: David Wise. Result: quiet modal material gains naturalistic layers as density rises. Play: begin sparse and pentatonic, then add repeats and higher notes gradually. Needs: adaptive layer system.
47. **Time-Cross Rhythm** — Reference: Yasunori Mitsuda. Result: compound-meter melody meets duple counter-rhythms. Play: repeat a six- or twelve-beat cell with strong internal accents. Needs: simultaneous meters; transport required.
48. **Crystal Chorale** — Reference: Nobuo Uematsu. Result: memorable melody grows into harmonic-minor chorale and octave answers. Play: clear four- or eight-bar phrases with held cadence notes. Current engine baseline.
49. **Kingdom Counterline** — Reference: Yoko Shimomura. Result: lyrical lead gains urgent inner lines and dramatic harmonic turns. Play: a memorable theme with expressive leaps, dynamics, and phrase-end rests. Needs: motif-aware counterlines and harmonic trajectory.
50. **Rust and Static** — Reference: Akira Yamaoka. Result: fragile fragments meet unstable clusters, shadows, and empty space. Play: isolated notes, slides, tritones, muted attacks, unpredictable pauses. Needs: bounded stochastic clusters and density safety.

## Baseline operational set

The first data-driven implementation must research and make these twelve honest and operational before introducing new engines: 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 14, 23, 25, 27, 36, 43, and 48. After all twelve pass automated acceptance, execution stops for user performance testing and explicit approval.

28. **Third-Cycle Labyrinth** — Reference: John Coltrane. Result: tonal centers rotate through major thirds. Play: repeat a compact motif while harmony changes beneath it. Needs: harmonic timeline and key cycle.
29. **Shout Counterpoint** — Reference: Charles Mingus. Result: bass ostinato, gospel response, and unruly counterline. Play: forceful two-bar blues calls followed by a full response opening. Needs: pattern, response, and multiple groups.
30. **Free Quartet** — Reference: Ornette Coleman. Result: independent contours and tonal centers. Play: exploratory lines with wide leaps and pauses to answer the ensemble. Needs: per-lane tonal centers and controlled independence.
31. **Side-Slip Matrix** — Reference: Herbie Hancock. Result: quartal harmony slips a semitone outside and returns. Play: simple inside-key modal motif; let the preset supply outside motion. Needs: timed side-slip timeline.
32. **Harmonic Maze** — Reference: Wayne Shorter. Result: ambiguous movement among diatonic, hexatonic, whole-tone, and octatonic regions. Play: sustained unresolved cells that avoid obvious cadences. Needs: weighted harmonic-state graph.
33. **Metric Labyrinth** — References: Tigran Hamasyan, Vijay Iyer. Result: percussive counterpoint across uneven groupings. Play: repeat an exact accented figure in 5, 7, or grouped 4/4. Needs: odd-meter pattern lanes; transport required.
34. **Chamber Sky** — References: Maria Schneider, Kenny Wheeler. Result: lyrical voices expand into airy ensemble harmony. Play: breath-shaped arcs, wide expressive intervals, soft attacks, long releases. Needs: groups, registers, and gradual entries.
35. **Elastic Counter-Groove** — References: Esperanza Spalding, Brad Mehldau, Robert Glasper. Result: syncopated harmony alternates with contrapuntal answers. Play: concise one- or two-bar riffs with deliberate holes. Needs: groove-aware response detection.

## Video game and interactive — 15

36. **Pixel Trio** — References: early console writing, Koji Kondo, Manami Matsumae. Result: melody, bass, and one counterline obey three-channel economy. Play: compact memorable single-note hooks with clear repeated rhythm. Current engine baseline.
37. **Fractured Crystal** — Reference: Disasterpeace, especially FEZ's constraint-driven linear writing. Result: a tiny motif fractures into limited-voice ostinatos and modal echoes. Play: repeat a three-to-five-note motif slowly, alter one note, and leave substantial air. Needs: bounded motif memory, sparse ostinato, and voice stealing.
38. **Summit Pulse** — Reference: Lena Raine. Result: intimate improvisatory melody grows into rhythmic upper layers. Play: begin softly with hesitant fragments and increase register, velocity, and repetition. Needs: intensity sensing and adaptive scenes.
39. **Adaptive Pilgrim** — References: Austin Wintory, Jessica Curry, Gareth Coker. Result: arrangement follows the emotional intensity arc. Play: isolated sustained notes, then longer/louder phrases, then withdraw. Needs: continuous intensity analysis and scene morphing.
40. **Ash and Ember** — References: Darren Korb, Ashley Barrett. Result: rough modal riffs receive acoustic, metallic, and vocal-like answers. Play: gritty short riffs, strong downbeats, slides, dramatic pauses. Needs: riff-response patterns; sound remains a separate suggestion.
41. **Blocks at Dusk** — Reference: C418. Result: sparse figures accumulate soft extended harmony. Play: two or three gentle notes repeated with small variations and long decay space. Needs: sparse-loop lane and probabilistic entry.
42. **Clockwork Stars** — Reference: Ben Prunty. Result: recurring motifs reappear across registers and counter-rhythms. Play: repeat a clean four-to-eight-note motif while preserving its rhythm. Needs: motif identity and recurrence tracking.
43. **Hollow Choir** — Reference: Christopher Larkin. Result: dark minor melody expands into distant chorale and counterline. Play: singable minor phrases, held destinations, long pauses. Current engine baseline; register groups improve it.
44. **Memory Weave** — Reference: Toby Fox. Result: two learned themes return transformed and combined. Play: teach two clearly distinct motifs, repeating each twice with a pause. Needs: named motif slots and combination.
45. **Neon Noir** — Reference: Shoji Meguro. Result: minor jazz-funk harmony with chromatic passing motion and rhythmic responses. Play: tight syncopated riffs, repeated notes, short chromatic runs. Needs: groove pattern, approaches, bass response.
46. **Forest Layer Unfold** — Reference: David Wise. Result: quiet modal material gains naturalistic layers as density rises. Play: begin sparse and pentatonic, then add repeats and higher notes gradually. Needs: adaptive layer system.
47. **Time-Cross Rhythm** — Reference: Yasunori Mitsuda. Result: compound-meter melody meets duple counter-rhythms. Play: repeat a six- or twelve-beat cell with strong internal accents. Needs: simultaneous meters; transport required.
48. **Crystal Chorale** — Reference: Nobuo Uematsu. Result: memorable melody grows into harmonic-minor chorale and octave answers. Play: clear four- or eight-bar phrases with held cadence notes. Current engine baseline.
49. **Kingdom Counterline** — Reference: Yoko Shimomura. Result: lyrical lead gains urgent inner lines and dramatic harmonic turns. Play: a memorable theme with expressive leaps, dynamics, and phrase-end rests. Needs: motif-aware counterlines and harmonic trajectory.
50. **Rust and Static** — Reference: Akira Yamaoka. Result: fragile fragments meet unstable clusters, shadows, and empty space. Play: isolated notes, slides, tritones, muted attacks, unpredictable pauses. Needs: bounded stochastic clusters and density safety.

## Baseline operational set

The first data-driven implementation must research and make these twelve honest and operational before introducing new engines: 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 14, 23, 25, 27, 36, 43, and 48. After all twelve pass automated acceptance, execution stops for user performance testing and explicit approval.

# Phase 10.2 Preset Research Pack Template

A public reference is not permission to reduce an artist to one scale or chord trick. Each operational preset needs three independent reports and a parent synthesis showing what the referenced style actually does, how it changes through time, and which parts Contrapunk can represent honestly.

## Required research roles

### A. Artist/style historian and primary-source researcher

Study authoritative sources, score-based analyses, institutional archives, treatises, and composer interviews where available.

Required sections:

1. **Scope and corpus** — name the works, recordings, scores, periods, or interviews used. Do not claim a whole-career style from one famous piece.
2. **Historical and aesthetic context** — what problem or tradition the artist was engaging with.
3. **Career/style evolution** — early, middle, late, project-specific, or medium-specific changes. State which period the preset references.
4. **Persistent traits versus period traits** — separate recurring concerns from techniques used only in selected works.
5. **Relationship to peers/tradition** — what is shared vocabulary and what is unusually characteristic.
6. **Common caricatures to avoid** — simplistic claims, genre stereotypes, or fan shorthand unsupported by evidence.
7. **Primary evidence** — cited URLs/publications and relevant work/measure/timestamp references where possible.
8. **Confidence and gaps** — high/medium/low confidence by claim.

### B. Music-theory and temporal-behavior researcher

Translate the scoped style into musical behavior, especially how it develops and moves rather than a static chord/scale snapshot.

Required dimensions:

- tonal center, modality, chromaticism, tuning;
- interval and chord vocabulary, spacing, inversion, doubling, tension/resolution;
- melodic contour, motivic construction, repetition, transformation, ornament;
- voice motion, independence, imitation, contrary/oblique/parallel behavior;
- rhythm, meter, subdivision, swing, accent, phase, polymeter;
- phrase length, density, silence, cadence, formal pacing;
- register, texture, orchestration/voice-role relationships;
- dynamics and articulation when they affect arrangement behavior;
- interaction between layers;
- **within-phrase evolution:** how the texture changes from attack to continuation to cadence;
- **across-section evolution:** how material accumulates, fragments, modulates, thins, returns, or transforms;
- **career/period evolution:** which theoretical rules belong to the selected period.

Deliverables:

1. A concise set of testable stylistic invariants.
2. Parameters that may vary without losing identity.
3. Behaviors that would make the result misleading.
4. A temporal state sketch, such as `Sparse → imitation → density peak → cadence`, with triggers.
5. Two or more short abstract input/output examples in scale degrees and beats; do not copy copyrighted melodies.
6. Mapping to existing HarmonyEngine/Lane capabilities and clearly named gaps.
7. Citations, confidence, and competing interpretations.

### C. Performer and interaction researcher

Determine how a live guitarist or keyboardist can evoke the researched behavior through Contrapunk rather than expecting the preset to manufacture it from arbitrary input.

Required sections:

1. Best source gesture: single notes, motif, riff, sustained tone, or chord.
2. Suggested register, tempo range, note lengths, articulation, dynamics, density, and silence.
3. Transport dependency and rhythmic precision requirements.
4. How the player should develop material over a phrase or section.
5. Listening/responding instructions: what generated layer to wait for before continuing.
6. Guitar-specific constraints under the clean-monophonic claim.
7. Keyboard-specific opportunities and chord-density limits.
8. Failure gestures that create mud, note storms, or stylistic contradiction.
9. Plain-language **Play it like** prompt plus expanded guidance.
10. A 30–60 second user acceptance exercise.

## Parent synthesis (`synthesis.md`)

The parent reads all three reports and records:

1. **Referenced scope** — artist/work/period actually represented.
2. **Style thesis** — one paragraph describing the sound and its temporal movement.
3. **Invariants** — rules the implementation must preserve.
4. **Evolution model** — phrase and section states, transitions, and triggers.
5. **Caricatures/rejected shortcuts** — tempting but misleading implementations.
6. **Contrapunk mapping** — exact scale, harmony, voice, Hold, lane, mix, timing, and capability values.
7. **Approximation statement** — what the engine cannot reproduce and how UI copy remains honest.
8. **Performer contract** — final short and expanded Play guidance.
9. **Acceptance examples** — abstract test inputs, expected relationships/evolution, and lifecycle expectations.
10. **Research traceability** — cited sources, report paths, confidence, and unresolved disagreements.
11. **Decision** — `ready_for_implementation`, `needs_more_research`, or `reject_as_misleading`.

## Multiple-reference presets

When a preset cites multiple artists, reports must not blend them indiscriminately. Identify:

- each artist's relevant period and technique;
- the documented intersection that motivates the preset;
- meaningful differences deliberately excluded;
- why the resulting preset is a coherent technique rather than a generic average.

## Research quality gate

A report fails when it:

- treats one scale, instrument, or famous work as an artist's entire style;
- lacks authoritative citations;
- describes only static harmony and not temporal evolution;
- copies protected melodic material rather than using abstract examples;
- cannot translate claims into performer guidance or testable engine behavior;
- contradicts another report without surfacing the disagreement;
- claims exact imitation when the implementation is only a bounded arrangement approximation.

Sicut cervus is a motet for four voices by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina. It sets the beginning of Psalm 42, Psalmus XLI in the Latin version of the Psalterium Romanum rather than the Vulgate Bible. The incipit is "Sicut cervus desiderat ad fontes" (As the deer desires the fountains) followed by a second part (secunda pars) "Sitivit anima mea" (My soul thirsts). It has become one of Palestrina's most popular motets, regarded as a model of Renaissance polyphony, expressing spiritual yearning.

The incipit is "Sicut cervus desiderat ad fontes" (As the deer desires the fountains) followed by a second part (secunda pars) "Sitivit anima mea" (My soul thirsts). It has become one of Palestrina's most popular motets, regarded as a model of Renaissance polyphony, expressing spiritual yearning.

Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (between 3 February 1525 and 2 February 1526 – 2 February 1594) was an Italian composer of late Renaissance music. The central representative of the Roman School, with Orlande de Lassus and Tomás Luis de Victoria, Palestrina is considered the leading composer of late 16th-century Europe. Palestrina was one of the few Renaissance composers never entirely forgotten, but it was the so-called "Palestrinian style" of counterpoint—especially as codified by Johann Josep
Source: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina)

This study offers analysis-based explanations of the construction of points of imitation in Palestrina's First Book of Four-Voice Motets. The traditional view that musical sense is based on repetition seems almost irrelevant to this repertoire, and the wonderfully unpredictable arrangement of thematic entries has seemed a mark of Palestrina's greatness. The inscription on an old portrait of him in the muniment room of the Pontifical Chapel at the Quirinal states that he died at about 80 years of age in 1594, and if this were true he would have been born in 1514 or 1515. text:
# Introduction

## Introduction

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-1)Artificial intelligence methods have been used for decades to model music composition ([Fernández & Vico, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1613%2Fjair.3908)). Two general approaches have attracted particular attention, as they mimic two aspects of how humans learn to compose. Firstly, rules have been used for centuries for teaching composition. Some algorithmic composition methods model symbolic knowledge and rules, for example, constraint-based approaches and formal grammars. Secondly, composers learn from examples of existing music. Machine learning (ML) methods of algorithmic composition include Markov chains, and artificial neural networks.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-2)We aim at combining these two approaches by automatically learning compositional rules from music corpora. We use genetic programming (GP) ([Poli, Langdon & McPhee, 2008](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=A%20field%20guide%20to%20genetic%20programming&author=Poli&publication_year=2008)) for that purpose.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-3)The resulting rules are represented symbolically, and can thus be studied by humans (in contrast to, say, artificial neural networks), but the rules can also be integrated into algorithmic composition systems. Extracting rules automatically is useful, for example, for musicologists to better understand the style of certain corpora, and for composers who use computers as a creative partner (computer-aided composition). For computer scientists, it is a challenging application domain.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-4)The resulting rules can be used in existing rule-based approaches to algorithmic composition where multiple rules can be freely combined, for example, in constraint-based systems ([Anders & Miranda, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1145%2F1978802.1978809)). Rules derived by ML and rules programmed manually can be freely combined in such systems, and rules can address various aspects (e.g. rules on rhythm, melody, harmony, voice leading, and orchestration). Potentially, ML can be used to derive rules from a given corpus of music for aspects where we do not have rules yet, for example, how to rhythmically and melodically shape the development of a phrase in a certain style.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-5)This article describes a pilot project within the research programme described above. In this pilot, we automatically extract rules for the treatment of dissonances in Renaissance music using a corpus of movements from Palestrina masses. The treatment of such dissonances is rather well understood, which helps evaluating results. Nevertheless, this task is far from trivial, as it has to take various musical viewpoints into account (e.g. melodic interval sizes and directions, note durations, and metric positions). Results can be interesting and useful not only for musicologists and composers, but also for the commercially relevant field of music information retrieval to advance the still unsolved problem of automatic harmonic analysis of polyphonic music.

## Background

### Inductive logic programming

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-6)Symbolic compositional rules have been extracted by ML before, specifically with inductive logic programming (ILP). ILP ([Muggleton et al., 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10994-011-5259-2)) combines logic programming with ML in order to learn first-order logic formulas from examples. Background knowledge expressed in logic programmes can be taken into account.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-7)Inductive logic programming has been used for several musical applications. Closely related to our goal is the work of [Morales & Morales (1995)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Learning%20musical%20rules&author=Morales&publication_year=1995). Their system learnt standard counterpoint rules on voice leading, namely how to avoid open parallels. Other musical applications of ILP include the learning of harmonic rules that express differences between two music corpora, specifically Beatles songs (pop music) and the Real Book (jazz) ([Anglade & Dixon, 2008](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Characterisation%20of%20harmony%20with%20inductive%20logic%20programming&author=Anglade&publication_year=2008)), and music performance rules for piano ([Tobudic & Widmer, 2003](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Relational%20IBL%20in%20music%20with%20a%20new%20structural%20similarity%20measure&author=Tobudic&publication_year=2003)) and violin ([Ramirez et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.3233%2FIDA-2010-0440)).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-8)Numeric relations are difficult to deduce with ILP, as logic programming in general is very restricted in expressing numeric relations. We are specifically interested in also learning numeric relations besides logic relations, because our experience with constraint-based modelling of music composition makes us aware of their importance for compositional rules. For example, the size of melodic and harmonic intervals is important, and such quantities are best expressed numerically. Besides, we want to use learnt rules later with constraint programming, a programming paradigm with very good support for restricting numeric relations.

### Genetic programming

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-9)In this project we therefore use another approach. GP is a particular kind of evolutionary algorithm that is used for ML. In GP, a tree structure is learnt by repeated application of random changes (mutation and recombination) and by the selection of the best structures among a set of candidates (a population) according to some criterion. A candidate tree can be the representation of a computer program or a mathematical equation among other possibilities. Early seminal work on GP has been published by [Koza (1992)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Genetic%20programming:%20on%20the%20programming%20of%20computers%20by%20means%20of%20natural%20selection&author=Koza&publication_year=1992), a more recent practical introduction can be found in [Poli, Langdon & McPhee (2008)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=A%20field%20guide%20to%20genetic%20programming&author=Poli&publication_year=2008).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-10)A particularly important application of GP is symbolic regression. Symbolic regression infers a mathematical expression that best fits the given data. The mathematical expression is unrestricted except that a specified set of building blocks is used–operators like +, or standard mathematical functions. The trees that GP builds from these building blocks are representations of such mathematical expressions. Symbolic regression is a powerful method that has been used in various areas of science and engineering ([Poli, Langdon & McPhee, 2008](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=A%20field%20guide%20to%20genetic%20programming&author=Poli&publication_year=2008)), including a high-profile study where it was used to automatically deduce physical laws from experiments ([Schmidt & Lipson, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1126%2Fscience.1165893)).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-11)Genetic programming has been used for music composition before. [Spector & Alpern (1994)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Criticism,%20culture,%20and%20the%20automatic%20generation%20of%20artworks&author=Spector&publication_year=1994) propose a system that automatically generates computer programmes for composing four-measure bebop jazz melodies. The generated programmes combine a number of given functions, inspired by Jazz literature, that transform short melodies from Charlie Parker in various ways. The fitness of each programme is evaluated by a set of restrictions inspired by [Baker (1988)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=David%20Baker%E2%80%99s%20Jazz%20improvisation&author=Baker&publication_year=1988), which measure the balance of different aspects (e.g. tonal and rhythmic novelty).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-12)[Johanson & Poli (1998)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=GP-music:%20an%20interactive%20genetic%20programming%20system%20for%20music%20generation%20with%20automated%20fitness%20raters&author=Johanson&publication_year=1998) also propose a system that creates computer programmes for transforming short melodies, but they allow users to interactively rate the quality of the generated music. This proved a tedious process for users. Therefore they complement the user-rating with automatic fitness raters that learn from the user ratings.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-13)Previous applications of GP for music composition thus aimed at modelling the full composition process, where the fitness function had to judge the quality of the resulting music. Yet, the programmes resulting from the evolutionary algorithm are rather short, and they are thus limited in the compositional knowledge they can represent. Previous work therefore composed music by transforming pre-existing music.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-14)Instead, we are interested in learning compositional rules with GP that describe only a certain aspect of the resulting music. Such rules are relevant in their own right as a representation of compositional knowledge that can be complemented with further musical knowledge, for example, in music constraint programming systems with manually encoded musical rules.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-15)In this situation, the fitness function does not need to judge musical quality. Instead, it only needs to estimate how well the resulting rule fits the given positive examples and avoids the negative examples.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-16)As far as we know, GP has not yet been used for learning symbolic compositional rules, and therefore in this study we focus on a relatively well understood class of rules.

### Dissonances in Palestrina’s music

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-17)This project studies the dissonance treatment in Palestrina counterpoint with ML by automatically generating multiple symbolic rules that each constrain the treatment of a specific dissonance category (passing tones, suspensions etc.).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-18)[Jeppesen (1946)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=The%20style%20of%20Palestrina%20and%20the%20dissonance&author=Jeppesen&publication_year=1946), the seminal authority on Palestrina counterpoint, distinguishes three roles a dissonance can play in his music. Some dissonances are hardly noticeable on a weak beat used for connecting notes in smooth melodic lines (Jeppesen calls them dissonances as a secondary phenomenon); others occur at an accented beat and are clearly heard (dissonances as primary phenomenon); and finally—more rarely—dissonances can be used for an expressive effect.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-19)As an example, [Fig. 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-1) shows an excerpt from a Palestrina mass movement[1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-1) with several dissonance categories in close proximity. All dissonances are marked with a crossed notehead, and are labelled with their dissonance category. Passing tones (p.t.) and neighbour tones (n.t.) are short notes on a weak beat that link melodic tones (secondary phenomenon). By contrast, suspensions (s.) stand out; they occur on a strong beat and typically at longer notes.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-1)
[![Image 1: Palestrina excerpt with several dissonances: several passing tones (p.t.), a neighbour tone (n.t.), and a suspension (s.), from the Agnus of missa De Beata Marie Virginis (II), measures 24–26.](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-1-1x.jpg)](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-1-2x.jpg "View the full image")

#### Figure 1: Palestrina excerpt with several dissonances: several passing tones (p.t.), a neighbour tone (n.t.), and a suspension (s.), from the Agnus of missa De Beata Marie Virginis (II), measures 24–26.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-21)The five standard dissonance categories taught in Palestrina counterpoint classes are passing tone, neighbour tone, suspension, anticipation and cambiata ([Jeppesen, 1939](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Counterpoint:%20the%20polyphonic%20vocal%20style%20of%20the%20sixteenth%20century&author=Jeppesen&publication_year=1939)). Traditionally, these categories are introduced progressively in class for pedagogic reasons in so-called species counterpoint, for example, in the 1725 textbook by [Fux (1965)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=The%20study%20of%20counterpoint.%20from%20Johann%20Joseph%20Fux%E2%80%99s%20Gradus%20ad%20Parnassum&author=Fux&publication_year=1965), which is still widely used.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-22)An algorithm for automatically identifying dissonances in Renaissance counterpoint has been proposed by [Patrick & Strickler (1978)](https://doi.org/10.1007%2FBF02400106), but it implements knowledge on the standard dissonance categories and therefore we instead developed a custom algorithm. The actual music of Palestrina contains further dissonance categories, as shown by computational analysis ([Sigler, Wild & Handelman, 2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Schematizing%20the%20treatment%20of%20dissonance%20in%2016th-century%20counterpoint&author=Sigler&publication_year=2015)).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-23)Counterpoint composition has often been modelled in a rule-based way, together with the relevant dissonance treatment. Already the 1957 composition _Illiac Suite_, commonly recognised as the first computer-generated composition, implemented for its second experiment and movement four-part first species counterpoint with rules similar to Renaissance counterpoint rules ([Hiller & Isaacson, 1993](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Musical%20composition%20with%20a%20high-speed%20digital%20computer&author=Hiller&publication_year=1993)). As a model for first species counterpoint, this early work sidestepped the issue of dissonance treatment, though, by simply not allowing for any dissonances. [Ebcioglu (1980)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Computer%20counterpoint&author=Ebcioglu&publication_year=1980) proposed a system that implemented two-part florid counterpoint to a given cantus firmus with rules inspired by Renaissance counterpoint that stem from Joseph Marx and Charles Koechlin and are complemented by rules of the author. Standard dissonance categories like passing tones, neighbour tones and suspensions are implemented, and published results attest to the musical quality of the output. [Schottstaedt (1989)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Automatic%20counterpoint&author=Schottstaedt&publication_year=1989) followed the Palestrina counterpoint rules of [Fux (1965)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=The%20study%20of%20counterpoint.%20from%20Johann%20Joseph%20Fux%E2%80%99s%20Gradus%20ad%20Parnassum&author=Fux&publication_year=1965) very faithfully and implemented all of Fux’ five species for up to six voices with own rules added to get closer to Fux’ actual examples.

## Methods

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-24)For learning symbolic compositional rules we use a novel methodology that combines multiple established approaches. At first, dissonant notes are automatically labelled in a corpus of music by Palestrina with a custom algorithm. These dissonances are then automatically clustered into different dissonance categories (passing notes, suspensions etc.) with the clustering algorithm DBSCAN ([Ester et al., 1996](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Density-based%20algorithm%20for%20discovering%20clusters%20in%20large%20spatial%20databases%20with%20noise&author=Ester&publication_year=1996)). Finally, a rule is learnt for each of these categories with GP. Each rule states conditions that must hold between three consecutive melodic notes if the middle note is a dissonance. The rest of this section describes each of these steps in more detail.

### Annotation of dissonances

#### A custom algorithm for dissonance detection in Renaissance music

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-25)As a first step we automatically label dissonances in the music using a custom algorithm implemented with the music analysis environment music21 ([Cuthbert & Ariza, 2010](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=music21:%20a%20toolkit%20for%20computer-aided%20musicology%20and%20symbolic%20music%20data&author=Cuthbert&publication_year=2010)). For our purposes, it is better for the algorithm to leave a few complex dissonance categories undetected than to wrongly mark notes as dissonances that are actually not dissonant. Note that this algorithm does not implement any knowledge of the dissonance categories known to occur in Palestrina’s music.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-26)The analysis first ‘chordifies’ the score, that is, it creates a homorhythmic chord progression where a new chord starts whenever one or more notes start in the score, and each chord contains all the score notes sounding at that time. The result of the ‘chordification’ process on its own would loose all voice leading information (e.g. where voice crossing happens), but our algorithm processes those chords and the original polyphonic score in parallel and therefore such information is retained. The algorithm tracks which score notes form which chord by accessing the notes with the same start time (music21 parameter _offset_) as a given chord.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-27)The algorithm then loops through the chords. If a dissonant chord is found,[2](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-2) it tries to find which note(s) make it dissonant by testing whether the chord becomes consonant if the pitches of these note(s) are removed.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-29)Dissonances are more likely to occur on short notes in Palestrina, and sometimes multiple dissonant tones occur simultaneously. The algorithm tests whether individual notes (and pairs of simultaneously moving notes) are dissonant. The algorithm progresses in an order that depends on the notes’ duration and a parameter $m a x _ p a i r _ d u r$, which specifies the maximum duration of note pairs tested (in our analysis $m a x _ p a i r _ d u r$ equalled to a half note). In order to minimise mislabelling dissonances, the algorithm first tests all individual notes with a duration up to $m a x _ p a i r _ d u r$ in increasing order of their duration; then all note pairs in increasing order of their duration; and finally remaining individual notes in order of increasing duration.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-30)Suspensions are treated with special care. Remember that the algorithm processes the ‘chordified’ score and the actual score in parallel. As a preprocessing step, the algorithm merges tied score notes into single notes to simplify their handling. When the algorithm then loops through the chords and finds a dissonant note that started before the currently tested chord, it splits that note into two tied notes, and only the second note starting with the current chord is marked as dissonant.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-31)In order to avoid marking notes wrongly as dissonances, the algorithm does not test the following cases: any note longer than $m a x _ d i s s _ d u r$, a given maximum dissonance duration (we set it to a whole note); and any suspension where the dissonant part of the note would exceed the preceding consonant part, or it would exceed $m a x _ d i s s _ d u r$.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-32)For this pilot we arbitrarily selected the first 36 Agnus mass movements from the full corpus of Palestrina music that ships with music21.[3](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-3) All examples in that subcorpus happen to be in $_{2}^{4}$ ‘metre’ (tempus imperfectum, denoted with cut half circle), but our method does not depend on that.

#### Evaluation of the dissonance detection algorithm

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-34)We evaluated results by manually ‘eyeballing’ a sample of scores with marked dissonances. The dissonance detection appears to work rather well; only very few notes were found wrongly labelled as a dissonance during our manual examination.[4](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-4)

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-36)[Figure 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-1) shows an example where dissonances would not be correctly labelled by our algorithm. The first two passing tones (eighth notes) are correctly labelled in [Fig. 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-1), but our algorithm would instead label the D in the soprano as a dissonance. The problem here is that when the two correct dissonances are removed, the resulting ‘chord’ A–D is a fourth, which is still considered a dissonance in Renaissance music. Instead, if the soprano D is removed, the remaining chord C–A happens to be consonant. Also, sometimes a suspension is not correctly recognised and instead a wrong note is labelled, where the voice proceeds by a skip in shorter notes.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-37)To be on the safe side for our purposes of learning dissonance treatment, the algorithm therefore does not label all dissonances. For example, occasionally more than two dissonances occur simultaneously in Palestrina, for example, when three parts move with the same short rhythmic values or in a counterpoint of more than four voices. If the algorithm does not find tones that, when removed, leave a consonant chord, then no note is labelled as a dissonance (though the chord is marked for proofreading). Excluding dissonances with the parameter $m a x _ d i s s _ d u r$ avoided a considerable number of complex cases and otherwise wrongly labelled notes.[5](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-5)

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-39)Due to these precautions (avoiding wrongly labelled dissonances), due to the corpus (selected Agnus movements) and the frequency of certain dissonance categories in that corpus, only a subset of the standard dissonance categories were detected and learnt as rules in this project (see [Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-1)). This point is further discussed below in the section on the evaluation of the clustering. Also, because the wrongly labelled dissonances are relatively rare and do not show regular patterns, the cluster analysis sorts these cases into an outlier category, which we did not use for rule learning, further improving the quality of the marked dissonance collections.

#### Data given to machine learning

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-40)Instead of handing the ML algorithm only basic score information (e.g. note pitches and rhythmic values), we provide it with background knowledge (like melodic intervals and accent weights as described below), and that way guide the search process. For flexibility, we considered letting the ML algorithm directly access the music21 score data with a set of given interface functions (methods), but extracting relevant score information in advance is more efficient.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-41)Once dissonances are annotated in the score, only melodic data is needed for the clustering and later the ML. For simplicity we only used dissonances surrounded by two consonant notes (i.e. no consecutive dissonances like cambiatas).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-42)In order to control the differences in ‘key’ between pieces in the corpus, our algorithm computes ‘normalised pitch classes’, where 0 is the tonic of the piece, 1 a semitone above the tonic and so forth. For this purpose we need to compute the ‘key’ of each piece. We are not aware of any algorithm designed for classifying Renaissance modes, and we therefore settled on instead using the Krumhansl-Schmuckler key determination algorithm ([Krumhansl, 1990](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Cognitive%20foundations%20of%20musical%20pitch&author=Krumhansl&publication_year=1990)) with simple key correlation weightings by [Sapp (2011)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Computational%20methods%20for%20the%20analysis%20of%20musical%20structure&author=Sapp&publication_year=2011). While this approach is not able to recognise modes, it is at least able to control the differences in accidentals between pieces.[6](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-6)

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-44)We determine accent weights using music21’s function _getAccentWeight_, where the strongest beat on the first beat of a measure has the weight 1.0; strong beats within a measure (e.g. the third beat in $_{2}^{4}$ ‘metre’) the weight 0.5; the second and fourth beat in $_{2}^{4}$ metre the weight 0.25 and so on ([Ariza & Cuthbert, 2010](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Modeling%20beats,%20accents,%20beams,%20and%20time%20signatures%20hierarchically%20with%20music21%20meter%20objects&author=Ariza&publication_year=2010)).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-45)Intervals are measured in semitones, and durations in quarter note lengths of music21, where 1 means a quarter note, 2 a half note and so on.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-46)For simplicity we left ties out in this pilot. Suspensions are simply repeated tones, they are not tied over.

### Cluster analysis of dissonance categories

#### Analysis With DBSCAN algorithm

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-47)For each dissonance, we provide the clustering algorithm with the following features: the sum of the durations of the previous, current, and next note (the reason for including this feature instead of including all note durations is explained in the following ‘Discussion’ section); the melodic interval from the previous note (measured in semitones), and the interval to the next note; the ‘normalised’ pitch class of the dissonance (i.e. 0 is the ‘tonic’ etc.); and the accent weight of the dissonance. Before clustering, all data for each feature is normalised such that its mean is 0.0 and its standard deviation is 1.0.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-48)The data is clustered using the DBSCAN algorithm ([Ester et al., 1996](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Density-based%20algorithm%20for%20discovering%20clusters%20in%20large%20spatial%20databases%20with%20noise&author=Ester&publication_year=1996)) as implemented in the scikit-learn library ([Pedregosa et al., 2011](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Scikit-learn:%20machine%20learning%20in%20Python&author=Pedregosa&publication_year=2011)). This clustering algorithm does not require setting the number of clusters in advance, and can find clusters of arbitrary shape as it is based on the density of points. Here, we set the minimum number of neighbours required to identify a point as a core cluster point to 10, and the maximum neighbour distance to 0.7 based on initial runs and the desire to keep the number of clusters in a reasonable range. Points that lie in low density regions of the sample space are recognised as outliers by DBSCAN, and are ignored in the subsequent rule learning step.

#### Clustering results and discussion

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-49)In order to evaluate the clustering results, we automatically labelled each dissonance in the score with its dissonance category (cluster number), and then created a new score for each cluster number into which all short melodic score snippets that contain this dissonance were collected (one-measure snippets, except where the dissonance occurs at measure boundaries). We then evaluated the clustering results by eyeballing those collections of score snippets[7](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-7) .

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-51)Initially, the importance of note durations for the clustering was rated too highly, because the clustering took more duration parameters into account (one for every note) than other parameters (e.g. pitch intervals between notes). As a result, one cluster contained primarily dissonances at half notes and another dissonances at shorter notes, which was not useful for our purposes. Therefore, we aggregated the duration information, and adjusted the DBSCAN parameters as described above, after which clustering worked very well.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-52)In the selected corpus only the following main dissonance categories are found: passing tones downwards on a weak beat (863 cases); passing tones upwards on a weak beat (643 cases); suspensions on the strong beat 3 in $_{2}^{4}$ ‘metre’ (313 cases); suspensions on the strong beat 1 (265 cases); and lower neighbour tones on a weak beat (230 cases).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-53)[Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-1) summarises the distinguishing features of the dissonance categories as found in clusters C0–C4, for which we learnt rules. Each row in the table describes a separate dissonance category as recognised by the clustering algorithm. The first interval indicates the melodic interval into the dissonance, and the second the interval from the dissonance to the next note. Metric position and duration are features of the dissonant note itself.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-54)Other dissonance categories like upper neighbour tones, anticipations and cambiatas do not occur in the ML training set. Either they do not exist in the first 36 Agnus mass movements of the music21 Palestrina corpus that we used, or they were excluded in some way. We only use dissonances surrounded by consonances (which excludes cambiatas). Also, we did not use the set of outliers (189 cases), which as expected, has no easily discernible common pattern. Among these outliers are wrongly labelled dissonances, upper neighbour tones, and a few further cases of the above main categories. There are also two small further clusters with lower neighbour tones (C5, 25 cases), and passing tones upwards (C6, 11 cases) that were discarded as they were considered to be too small, and cover categories that are already covered by larger clusters.

### Learning of rules

#### Training set

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-55)To initiate rule learning, our algorithm compiles for each identified cluster (dissonance category) a set of three-note-long learning examples with a dissonance as middle note. All dissonances that have been assigned to that particular cluster are used as positive examples.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-56)Then, four sets of negative examples are generated. Note that the generation of negative examples does not take any knowledge about the problem domain into account. A similar approach can also be used for learning rules on other musical aspects. The first set is a random sample of dissonances that have been assigned to other clusters. The second set is a random sample of three-tone-examples without any dissonance taken from the corpus. The third set consists of examples where all features are set to random values drawn from a uniform distribution over the range of possible values for each feature. The fourth set consists of slightly modified random samples from the set of positive examples. Two variations are generated for each chosen example. Firstly, either the interval between the dissonant tone and the previous note or the interval to the next note is changed by ±2 semitones (with equal probabilities). Secondly, one of the three note durations is either halved or doubled (with equal probabilities). Both modifications are stored separately in the fourth set of negative examples.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-57)The algorithm aims to create 20% of the number of positive examples for each set of negative examples, but will generate at least 200 examples (100 for the first set due to possible low availability of these examples) and at most 500. These numbers represent mostly a trade-off between accuracy of training/measurement and computation time, and we expect a similar performance if these values are changed within reasonable ranges.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-58)Once all example sets have been constructed, each example receives a weight such that the total weight of the positive examples is 1.0, and the total weight of each of the four sets of negative examples is 0.25 (within each set, the weights are the same for all examples). When measuring classification accuracy of a rule during the learning process, each positive example that is classified correctly counts +1 times the example weight, whereas each negative example that is erroneously classified as positive example counts −1 times the example weight. Thus, the accuracy score is a number between −1.0 and 1.0, with 0.0 expected for a random classifier.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-59)Please note that with a low probability a randomly generated negative example can be the same as a positive example. Here, we consider this as a small amount of noise in the measurement, but for future experiments it is possible to filter these out at the expense of run time.

#### Learning process

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-60)We use strongly typed GP as implemented in the Python library DEAP ([https://github.com/deap/deap](https://github.com/deap/deap)) ([Fortin et al., 2012](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=DEAP:%20evolutionary%20algorithms%20made%20easy&author=Fortin&publication_year=2012)) with the types float and Boolean (integers are translated to floats). The following functions can occur as parent nodes in the tree that represents a learnt rule.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-61)Logical operators: $\lor$ (or), $\land$ (and), $\neg$ (not), $\rightarrow$ (implication), $\leftrightarrow$ (equivalence)

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-62)Arithmetic operators and relations: $+$, $-$, $\cdot$ (multiplication), $/$ (division), $-$ (unary minus), $=$, $<$, $>$

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-63)Conditional: $i f _ t h e n _ e l s e \left(\right. \langle b o o l e a n \rangle$, $\langle f l o a t \rangle$, $\langle f l o a t \rangle \left.\right)$

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-64)Terminal nodes in a ‘rule tree’ can be either input variables (like the duration of a note or the interval to its predecessor or successor) or ephemeral random constants (constants whose values can be changed by mutations). The following input variables can be used in the learnt rules: the duration of the dissonant note ($d u r a t i o n_{i}$), its predecessor ($d u r a t i o n_{i - 1}$) and successor ($d u r a t i o n_{i + 1}$); the normalised pitch class of the dissonance; the intervals[8](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-8) between the dissonance and its predecessor ($i n t e r v a l_{p r e}$) and successor ($i n t e r v a l_{s u c c}$); and the accent weight of the dissonance ($a c c e n t W e i g h t_{i}$). As for the ephemeral random constants, there are the Boolean constants $t r u e$ and $f a l s e$, as well as integer constants in the form of values between 0 and 13. The notation given here is the notation shown later in learnt rule examples.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-66)There are many choices of operators and parameters that can be used with GP. Here, we follow standard approaches that are commonly used in the GP practitioners’ community, and/or are DEAP defaults, unless otherwise noted. The population is created using ramped half-and-half initialisation, after which at each generation the following operators are applied. For selection, we use tournament selection with a tournament size of 3. For mutation, there is a choice between three operators: standard random tree mutation (95% probability), a duplication operator that creates two copies of the tree and connects them using the $\land$ operator (2.5%), and a similar duplication operator using the $\lor$ operator (2.5%). For recombination, there is again a choice between standard tree exchange crossover (95%), an operator that returns the first individual unchanged, and a combination of the first and second individual using the $\land$ operator (2.5%), and a similar operator using $\lor$ (2.5%). While random tree mutation and tree exchange crossover are commonly used, we designed the other operators to encourage the emergence of rules that are conjunctions or disjunctions of more simple rules, which is a useful format for formal compositional rules. Without these operators, it would be extremely unlikely that a new simple rule could be evolved without disrupting the already evolved one, or that different already evolved rules could be combined as a whole. A static depth limit of 25 is imposed on the evolving trees to avoid stack overflows and exceedingly long execution times.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-67)A population of 100 individuals is evolved for 1,000 generations. The fitness assigned to an individual is 10 times its accuracy score (described above) minus 0.001 times the size of its tree. That way, among two rules with equal classification accuracy, the more compact rule has a slight fitness advantage. We introduced this as a measure to slow down the growth of the trees during evolution (known as ‘bloat control’ in the field of GP, although the effect of this particular measure is not very strong). We performed five runs for every cluster. They use the same set of learning examples, but find different rules nonetheless due to the stochastic nature of GP.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-68)After a run is finished, the best rule evolved in that run is output together with its classification accuracy scores[9](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fn-9) .

## Results

### Quantitative evaluation

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-70)The quality of the rule learning process as implemented by GP is evaluated by measuring the accuracies of the best evolved rules (see [Fig. 2](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-2)). It can be seen that the accuracies for positive examples are better than 98% in most cases, the accuracies on negative examples from other clusters are mostly better than 99%, the accuracies on negative examples without dissonances are mostly better than 94%, the accuracies on random counterexamples are close to 100%, and the accuracies for modified positive examples are mostly better than 94% but around 89% for the first cluster. When plotting overall accuracy scores against the sizes of the rules’ corresponding GP trees ([Fig. 3](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-3)), it can be seen that rules for the same cluster achieve similar accuracy scores despite different sizes. However, across clusters, there seems to be a negative correlation between accuracy and rule size. The most plausible explanation seems to be that larger clusters are more difficult to describe, resulting both in larger rule sizes and lower accuracy scores ([Fig. 4](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-4)). The accuracy of some negative examples (i.e. examples without dissonances, and modified positive examples) might be lower, because some of them may accidentally match the pattern of positive examples.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-2)
[![Image 2: Accuracies achieved by the champions of the genetic programming runs on the various parts of the training set.](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-2-1x.jpg)](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-2-2x.jpg "View the full image")

#### Figure 2: Accuracies achieved by the champions of the genetic programming runs on the various parts of the training set.

(A) postive examples; (B) counterexamples from other clusters; (C) harmonic counterexamples; (D) random counterexamples; (E) randomly modified positive examples. The means are indicated by blue bars. C0–C6 denotes the clusters found by DBSCAN. These clusters correspond to different dissonance categories (see [Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-1)). C5 and C6 are two small clusters that were disregarded in the end (see discussion at the end of section ‘Clustering Results and Discussion’ above).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-3)
[![Image 3: Accuracy score vs tree size for the evolved solutions from all runs.](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-3-1x.jpg)](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-3-2x.jpg "View the full image")

#### Figure 3: Accuracy score vs tree size for the evolved solutions from all runs.

Clusters are denoted by their respective numbers.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#fig-4)
[![Image 4: Accuracy score (A) and tree size (B) vs cluster size.](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-4-1x.jpg)](https://dfzljdn9uc3pi.cloudfront.net/2019/cs-244/1/fig-4-2x.jpg "View the full image")

#### Figure 4: Accuracy score (A) and tree size (B) vs cluster size.

Clusters are denoted by their respective numbers.

### Qualitative evaluation

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-74)We evaluated the suitability of the evolved rules for describing dissonances by using them as melodic constraints in small constraint problems implemented with the music constraint system Cluster Engine ([http://github.com/tanders/clusterengine](http://github.com/tanders/clusterengine)), which is a revision of the solver PWMC ([Sandred, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1162%2Fcomj.2010.34.2.8)). Both these solvers are libraries of the visual programming and composition environment PWGL ([Laurson, Kuuskankare & Norilo, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1162%2Fcomj.2009.33.1.19)). The constraint problems consist of only three notes with the middle note as the dissonance and surrounding rests as padding so that these notes can occur freely on any beat.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-75)For each learnt rule (five per cluster resulting from the five runs reported above) we generated 15 random solutions (an arbitrary number). We examined these solutions in common music notation, and appraised how well they complied with the respective dissonance category. Specifically, we checked whether the metric position and duration of the middle note (the dissonance) and the melodic intervals into and from this note are appropriate.

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#p-76)For each cluster (dissonance category) at least one learnt rule constrains the treatment of the dissonant middle note in a way that either fully complies with the features of the corresponding positive examples (see [Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-1) again), or is at least very close. In other words, this ‘best rule’ per cluster works either perfectly or at least rather well when used as a constraint for its dissonance category. [Table 2](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-2) shows how accurate the best rule of each dissonance category is by reporting the greatest deviation found in any solution among a set of 15 random solutions. The full qualitative evaluation results—together with the raw rule results—are available with the data provided with this paper (under _Resulting Rules and Evaluation_).

[](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-2)

Table 2:

Qualitative evaluation summary: greatest deviation found between features of positive examples (see [Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-1)) and solutions to best rule for each cluster.

| Cluster | Category | 1st interval | 2nd interval | Metric position | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C0 | Passing tones down | None | None | None | None |
| C1 | Passing tones up | None | None | None | None |
| C2 | Suspension on beat 3 | None | None | None | Small[a](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-2fn1) |
| C3 | Suspension on beat 1 | Small[b](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-2fn2) | None | None | Small[a](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244#table-2fn1) |
