# enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina

Questions I ask myself when contemplating whether an excerpt from music literature is appropriate for illustrative purposes in class include: Which elements are typical? Which elements are atypical? Which elements generally considered to be typical do not appear in this excerpt? _How_ typical are the typical elements? What is the distribution of typical elements, within an excerpt, a movement, or in different compositions? These questions often occur in relation to my counterpoint course regarding aspects of sixteenth-century style, and specifically concern the appearance of dissonance in the Palestrinian sacred repertoire. I decided, therefore, to make an enumeration of nine selected uses of dissonance in the Masses of Palestrina, and have found that such a study serves pedagogical purposes in at least five ways:

> 1. It provides sources in which there are several occurrences of any one specific device within a short span, useful as a resource for class illustration purposes.
> 
> 
> 2. It has provided the means to calculate a prototypical distribution of selected devices; that is, an average number of measures per movement and an average number of respective devices within the average number of measures. This has been used to select some movements approximating this prototypical distribution which can be employed for student analysis projects, in class, or on exams.
> 
> 
> 3. It provides a basis for judging the accuracy of generalizations regarding nonharmonic usage which are encountered in counterpoint texts and treatises.
> 
> 
> 4. It provides a basis for judging the "relative typicality" of the kind and amount of nonharmonic usage in selections included in anthologies.
> 
> 
> 5. Besides providing information regarding specific treatment of the various devices, it also provides sources to illustrate relatively uncommon occurrences.

The first step in the project was to complete a study of all the discrete three-voice sections in the Palestrina Masses, using the Fratelli Scalera complete edition as the source.[1](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x1) (Since there are no three-voice Masses, selected were those sections of complete Mass movements that are separate and that are reduced to three-voice texture, such as the _Crucifixus_ of the _Credo_, the _Pleni sunt coeli_ of the _Sanctus_, and the _Bendictus_.) There are 73 such sections, having a total of 2,894 bars, occurring in 46 different Masses.

In the second part of the study, all the four-voice movements of the four-voice Masses were examined. There are 40 four-voice Masses, with 210 four-voice movements, having a total of 18,313 bars. All movements constituting the Ordinary of the Mass were included; only those sections having other than four-voice texture were not included.

I chose to enumerate those devices which, in my experience, seem to need highlighting for the sake of the student, at the juncture in the sixteenth-century counterpoint course where nonharmonic usage is being considered. The devices chosen include five suspensions (namely, the 9-8, the 7-6, the 4-3, the 2-3, and the 2-1), the accented passing tone (that is, the quarter-note value in 4/2 meter), the consonant fourth, the _nota cambiata_, and the 6/5 harmonic combination. Not included are unaccented passing tones, neighboring tones, portamentos, or pairs of eighth notes. Each occurrence of each device was tabulated and was further categorized according to the number of voices sounding at the point of the dissonance. Additional information regarding specific details pertinent to the use of the devices was recorded separately for each movement.

For the three-voice study, statistical results were arrived at manually. Some have also been done manually for the four-voice study, but in addition the data have been recorded on a computer using a system known as INTERACT which has great flexibility for editing and printout format, and is also subject to a packaged statistical analysis program for calculating desired information. For the four-voice Masses, therefore, there is a printout which lists all movements of all Masses (alphabetically by Mass title) and includes the number of each of the respective devices in each movement, and of those in two-, three-, and four-voice texture. The ratio of number of devices to number of measures appears below each entry of raw data. Totals for all Masses appear at the end of the listing. A second printout is arranged by movement rather than by Mass title. Thus all the _Kyrie_ movements appear successively, followed by totals, then all the _Gloria_, _Credo_ and similar movements. All the ratios were sorted and the 14 which indicate the greatest frequency of occurrence appear on a third printout, thus providing a list of the 14 movements having the relatively largest number of occurrences in the relatively fewest number of measures for each device in each of the possibilities (total, two-, three-, and four-voice texture). While it is not possible to list all statistical details here, illustrations of some of the information which has resulted from the study are included.

One of the first items of interest is the rank order and total number of occurrences of the selected nine devices. These appear in Table 1.

**TABLE 1

TOTAL, RATIOS, AND PROTOTYPICAL DISTRIBUTION**

![Image 1: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl1.jpg)

The devices are listed in rank order, descending, from left to right, first for the three-voice sections, and then for the four-voice movements. The number of occurrences of each device is given, including a breakdown showing two-voice and three-voice usage in the three-voice sections, and two-, three-, and four-voice usage for the four-voice movements. It is probably no surprise that the 4-3 suspension ranks first, or that the 2-1 suspension ranks last, but the list of the remaining devices should be of interest, both for the order and the amounts as well as for the fact that with only the exception of the 2-3 suspension, the order stays the same for the use of devices in the three-voice sections and the use in four-voice movements. (The dotted line in the middle of the table calls attention to the shift in order for the 2-3 suspension). Notice also that the breakdown into subgroups according to the number of voices sounding (at the point the device occurs) provides interesting information. Other than what is obvious for the harmonic 6/5, no occurrences were found of the consonant fourth or the 2-1 suspension in two voices, and only two 9-8 suspensions were found in two voices, one in the three-voice sections and one in the four-voice movements. (Since there was only the one in the four-voice movements, it is not included in the information available on the computer printout, and the entry appears in parentheses on the table.) While the 2-3 is third in rank order for the total number of occurrences in three-voice texture, it has the highest number of two-voice occurrences—far more than the 7-6, for instance. However, in the four-voice movements, the two-voice occurrences of the 7-6 outnumber those of the 2-3 by 156 to 148. In the four-voice movements there are more 7-6's, harmonic 6/5's, 2-3's, and 2-1's in three voices than in four.

Also included in Table 1 is the ratio of the number of occurrences of each device to the total number of bars, rounded to whole numbers. In the three-voice study, for instance, the 4-3 suspension occurs on an average of once every five bars, the 7-6 once every 15 bars, etc., while in the four-voice study, the 4-3 occurs once every four bars, the 7-6 once every ten bars, etc. These ratios serve as the basis for comparisons, and as the basis for arriving at the prototypical distribution which is also shown. In the three-voice sections, for example, for the average length of a section, which is 40 bars, the averaged or prototypical distribution is eight 4-3 suspensions, three 7-6 suspensions, two 2-3 suspensions, two accented passing tones, two _nota cambiata_ figures, one harmonic 6/5, and no 9-8's, consonant fourths, or 2-1's. The information in the last column to the right shows the ratio of the total number of devices to the number of measures; in three-voice sections it is 1:2.25, in four-voice movements it is 1:1.96, indicating that the devices occur slightly more frequently in the four-voice movements than in the three-voice sections. Further discussion of the information on Table 1 will not be undertaken at this point, but the reader is encouraged to glean information from the Table as appropriate to meet needs and satisfy curiosity.

Examination of all the data recorded produced little information which could serve as the basis for suggesting tendencies or trends regarding the use of the nine devices. For instance, attention was given to changes that might occur, in some methodical pattern, throughout the compositional period. With one exception no such pattern emerged. The exception is that in the four-voice movements, 291 of the 593 _nota cambiata_ figures occur in the first seven four-voice Masses (from volumes one and four of the Fratelli Scalera complete edition) and the remainder are distributed among the other 33 Masses, thus reflecting a marked decline in the employment of the _cambiata_. In the three-voice study, one tabulation grouped the entries according to the two most common voice combinations: cantus-altus-tenor and altus-tenor-bassus. The resulting ratios are quite similar to the ratios of the complete totals and there are only two instances of a change in rank order: in the cantus-altus-tenor arrangement, there are a few more _nota cambiata_ figures than accented passing notes, and in the altus-tenor-bassus voicing there are two more 9-8 suspensions, than harmonic 6/5 combinations. Differentiation by text setting was also examined. In the three-voice study, separate totals were tabulated for the _Crucifixus_, the _Pleni sunt coeli_ and the _Benedictus_ settings. Again, with only a few instances of a slight shift in rank position, the resulting ratios are very similar to those for the totals. Totals for the four-voice study were computed by movement (all the _Kyrie_ movements, all the _Credo_ movements, etc.). These results appear in Table 2.

**TABLE 2

COMPARISON OF TOTALS OF ALL MOVEMENTS TO TOTALS BY TYPE OF MOVEMENT**

![Image 2: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl2.jpg)

Most ratios for the movements are quite similar to those for the total of all movements. The rank order changes are indicated by the encircling of an entry whose raw score is higher than that of the entry to its left. On the basis of the ratios appearing in the right hand "Totals" column, the generality can be made that there is a slightly greater frequency of the devices in the shorter movements (_Kyrie_, _Benedictus_, _Agnus Dei_) than there is in the longer movements (_Gloria_ and _Credo_), but the differences do not seem terribly significant.

Besides the numbers of occurrences of the devices, special conditions sometimes attendant to each respective device were recorded. Included in the four-voice study for example are instances such as 104 suspensions in which the resolution note is already present in an accompanying voice, 851 4-3 suspensions accompanied by the melodic 6-5, 26 9-8 suspensions in which the ninth is a minor ninth and not a major ninth, various harmonic combinations with the 2-3 suspension, 63 accented passing tones approached by parallel dissonance or by leap to a dissonance, aspects of the preparation and resolution of the 6/5 harmonic combination, and 36 consonant fourths preceded by the harmonic 6/5.

Also listed were instances of the use of double nonharmonic devices. In the basic tally, each part of a double nonharmonic device was counted individually (for instance, a 9-8/4-3 double suspension was tallied as one 9-8 and one 4-3); therefore it was necessary to keep separate information regarding all such occurrences. Results of this tabulation appear on Table 3.

**TABLE 3 

DOUBLE NON-HARMONIC DEVICES**

![Image 3: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl3.jpg)

Notice that the double suspensions are subdivided into specific combinations, that there are more double suspensions than double _nota cambiata_ figures or double accented passing tones, and that there are many more double suspensions in four-voice movements than in three, with a correspondingly greater frequency of occurrence. Obviously it is necessary to subtract the number of suspensions involved in combinations from the totals which appear in Table 2 to get the number of _single_ suspensions. For example, there are 193 4-3 suspensions in a double-suspension combination; therefore, of the total 4,681 4-3 suspensions, 4,488 are single suspensions.

Another item of interest is the number of _different_ devices in any one movement. Table 4 shows graphically the percentage of the number of movements with the respective number of different devices.

**TABLE 4 

PERCENTAGE OF NUMBER OF MOVEMENTS WITH 

RESPECTIVE NUMBER OF DIFFERENT DEVICES**

![Image 4: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl4.jpg)

For instance, the three-voice sections, only one, or one percent, has just two different devices; nine sections, or twelve percent have three different devices; thirteen, or eighteen percent have four different devices, etc. The largest percentage (i.e., 29 percent) of the three-voice sections contains just five different devices, and only one has all nine devices. (Frankly, for pedagogical purposes, I was hoping to find a few more with all nine.) In the four-voice movements, graphed at the bottom of Table 4, notice that the distribution among movements with five, six, seven, and eight different devices is quite evenly balanced, and that there are eighteen movements, or nine percent of the total, that have all nine devices.

Of the previously-mentioned five purposes which the results of the study could serve, the first is to provide sources with many occurrences of each respective device. Specific references from the three-voice sections are in Table 5, and references from the four-voice movements are in Table 6.

**TABLE 5 

LARGE NUMBER OF OCCURRENCES OF 

EACH RESPECTIVE DEVICE**

![Image 5: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl5.jpg)

**TABLE 6 

LARGE NUMBER OF OCCURRENCES OF 

EACH RESPECTIVE DEVICE**

![Image 6: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl6Revised.jpg)

The left column of each Table gives the average number of occurrences per movement of each device so that this may be compared to the number in these selected movements. Then for each device the movement with the largest number of that device is given, followed by one or two more examples that have, for that device, a frequency ratio of number of occurrences to number of bars which reflects a relatively large number of occurrences in a relatively few number of measures. The right hand column of each table contains the number of movements in which there are _none_ of each of the respective devices. These tables should provide valuable resource information for those who may be teaching sixteenth-century counterpoint and are searching for illustrations of specific individual devices from the Palestrinian literature.

The second purpose of the study is the selection of some movements which approximate the prototypical distribution of the devices. Table 7 has selections from the three-voice sections.

**TABLE 7

EXAMPLES WHICH APPROXIMATE THE PROTOTYPICAL DISTRIBUTION3-VC**

![Image 7: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl7Revised.jpg)

The prototypical distribution appears first, again to assist in making comparisons. Included within the three-voice selections is the _Benedictus_ from the Mass _De feria_, from volume six of the complete edition, which is the only one of the 73 three-voice sections that contains at least one occurrence of all nine devices. Information for the four-voice movements is in Table 8.

**TABLE 8

EXAMPLES WHICH APPROXIMATE THE PROTOTYPICAL DISTRIBUTION4-VC**

![Image 8: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl8.jpg)

The first four examples all contain one of each of the nine devices. The last three are selected from those movements that lack only the 2-1 suspension, since this reflects the arrangement in the prototypical distribution.

The third purpose is to use the information to evaluate generalizations found in counterpoint books. Statements that have to do with some aspect of the amount or relative degree of use of some of these devices may be found in books by authors such as Kitson, Merritt, Jeppesen, Soderlund, N.K. Andrews, Bassett, and Benjamin. For the most part the statistics do support the statements that one encounters, but sometimes the information is incomplete, misleading, or incorrect. A few selected examples must suffice to illustrate the possibilities of statement evaluation. H.K. Andrews writes, "the most commonly found suspended dissonances above the bass . . . (are the) 7-6 and 4-3."[2](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x2)

The information on Table 1 does not support this, but in this case as well as in several others the statistics lend further insight, because it would be appropriate to point out that many _more_ examples of 4-3 than 7-6 occur, and that there is a difference depending on whether two-voice texture or texture with three or more voices is being considered.

Concerning double suspensions Bassett writes, "Of all the possible double suspensions, only two are easily found: the 7-6/4-3 and the 9-8/4-3."[3](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x3) These two double suspensions are indeed those which occur most frequently in the four-voice Masses, which can be verified by referring to Table 3. However, it does seem that authors are more likely to point out those items that occur seldom or never. For instance, immediately following the previously quoted statement in the Bassett manual concerning the 7-6/4-3 and 9-8/4-3 double suspensions, he says, "The 9-8/7-6 double suspension, while theoretically quite acceptable, was for some reason not used by Palestrina."[4](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x4) This unfortunately, is not a true statement, since as can be seen from Table 3, one example was found in the three-voice study and four examples were found in the four-voice study. The last example of a generality from a text is on the same subject of double suspensions. Benjamin says that the 4-3/2-1 is among the typical double suspensions, but that the 7-6/4-3 is rare (because "it produces ineffective parallel fourths").[5](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x5) This gives an impression which is just the opposite of what actually occurs, since in the four-voice Masses, there are 111 7-6/4-3 double suspensions and only 10 which are the 4-3/2-1 combination. While the process of statement evaluation may have to take into account factors beyond total of occurrences (as was done during the course of this study), it is possible that in many instances information contained in the tables accompanying this article will be applicable.

The fourth of the five purposes is to provide a basis for comparison to selections in anthologies or texts, assuming that among other things the occurrence and distribution of dissonance is a consideration in making a choice of a composition to use. The prototypical distribution (see Table 1) provides a standard against which to compare the number of measures and number of nonharmonic devices found in such sources. As part of this study, 19 examples of sixteenth-century sacred polyphony in three voices from nine different anthologies or texts were examined. The distribution of dissonance within most of the 19 examples does not come very close to the prototypical distribution, but of the 19 examples, 9 are three-voice sections from the Palestrinian Masses, and two of these are included on Table 7 as examples which approximate the prototypical distributions. One is the _Benedictus_ from the Mass _Gabriel archangelus_ and it is found in two books, in the collection of Soderlund[6](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x6) and in the text by Benjamin.[7](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x7) The other selection is the _Benedictus_ from the Mass _Repleatur os meum laude_. This is also found in the Soderlund collection,[8](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x8) and is included as well in the AtKisson text.[9](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x9) The intent regarding this fourth purpose is not to suggest that selections in texts and anthologies are, are not, or should be based on the distribution of dissonance, but rather it is to suggest that it may often be in order for a teacher to call to the attention of students that certain aspects of a composition may contain some elements (or have omissions) which are not necessarily representative of a larger corpus of works, and in the case of Palestrina Mass movements, the information gathered enables one to be more specific concerning the kinds and amounts of nonharmonic devices which are encountered.

The fifth and last purpose is to accumulate a list of sources that illustrate devices used so seldom that they are considered rare or exceptional. While it is not the purpose of this report to give detailed information regarding these cases, the types of items include 4-5 or 7-8 lower-voice suspensions, the suspended diminished fifth, augmented triads in 6/3 position, diminished triads in 5/3 position (which are on a weak beat, and do not follow a 6/5), four eighth notes in a row, quarter note tones, high-note law exceptions, use of the Landini sixth melodic pattern, leaps to and/or from a dissonance, an upper neighbor tone in a half-note value, and syllable change with quarter notes.

A brief idea of the analytical study undertaken has been presented, along with some examples of specific resource information. Admittedly, further work is possible, including the enumeration of devices in five-voice (and more) Masses, in works other than Masses, and in works of other composers of the period, in both sacred and secular categories. But what has been done should help to substantiate the premise that the process of enumeration can play an important role in the ultimate product of illumination.

[2](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#2)Herbert Kennedy Andrews, _An Introduction to the Technique of Palestrina_ (London: Novello and Company, 1958), p. 117.

# enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina

Questions I ask myself when contemplating whether an excerpt from music literature is appropriate for illustrative purposes in class include: Which elements are typical? Which elements are atypical? Which elements generally considered to be typical do not appear in this excerpt? _How_ typical are the typical elements? What is the distribution of typical elements, within an excerpt, a movement, or in different compositions? These questions often occur in relation to my counterpoint course regarding aspects of sixteenth-century style, and specifically concern the appearance of dissonance in the Palestrinian sacred repertoire. I decided, therefore, to make an enumeration of nine selected uses of dissonance in the Masses of Palestrina, and have found that such a study serves pedagogical purposes in at least five ways:

> 1. It provides sources in which there are several occurrences of any one specific device within a short span, useful as a resource for class illustration purposes.
> 
> 
> 2. It has provided the means to calculate a prototypical distribution of selected devices; that is, an average number of measures per movement and an average number of respective devices within the average number of measures. This has been used to select some movements approximating this prototypical distribution which can be employed for student analysis projects, in class, or on exams.
> 
> 
> 3. It provides a basis for judging the accuracy of generalizations regarding nonharmonic usage which are encountered in counterpoint texts and treatises.
> 
> 
> 4. It provides a basis for judging the "relative typicality" of the kind and amount of nonharmonic usage in selections included in anthologies.
> 
> 
> 5. Besides providing information regarding specific treatment of the various devices, it also provides sources to illustrate relatively uncommon occurrences.

The first step in the project was to complete a study of all the discrete three-voice sections in the Palestrina Masses, using the Fratelli Scalera complete edition as the source.[1](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x1) (Since there are no three-voice Masses, selected were those sections of complete Mass movements that are separate and that are reduced to three-voice texture, such as the _Crucifixus_ of the _Credo_, the _Pleni sunt coeli_ of the _Sanctus_, and the _Bendictus_.) There are 73 such sections, having a total of 2,894 bars, occurring in 46 different Masses.

In the second part of the study, all the four-voice movements of the four-voice Masses were examined. There are 40 four-voice Masses, with 210 four-voice movements, having a total of 18,313 bars. All movements constituting the Ordinary of the Mass were included; only those sections having other than four-voice texture were not included.

I chose to enumerate those devices which, in my experience, seem to need highlighting for the sake of the student, at the juncture in the sixteenth-century counterpoint course where nonharmonic usage is being considered. The devices chosen include five suspensions (namely, the 9-8, the 7-6, the 4-3, the 2-3, and the 2-1), the accented passing tone (that is, the quarter-note value in 4/2 meter), the consonant fourth, the _nota cambiata_, and the 6/5 harmonic combination. Not included are unaccented passing tones, neighboring tones, portamentos, or pairs of eighth notes. Each occurrence of each device was tabulated and was further categorized according to the number of voices sounding at the point of the dissonance. Additional information regarding specific details pertinent to the use of the devices was recorded separately for each movement.

For the three-voice study, statistical results were arrived at manually. Some have also been done manually for the four-voice study, but in addition the data have been recorded on a computer using a system known as INTERACT which has great flexibility for editing and printout format, and is also subject to a packaged statistical analysis program for calculating desired information. For the four-voice Masses, therefore, there is a printout which lists all movements of all Masses (alphabetically by Mass title) and includes the number of each of the respective devices in each movement, and of those in two-, three-, and four-voice texture. The ratio of number of devices to number of measures appears below each entry of raw data. Totals for all Masses appear at the end of the listing. A second printout is arranged by movement rather than by Mass title. Thus all the _Kyrie_ movements appear successively, followed by totals, then all the _Gloria_, _Credo_ and similar movements. All the ratios were sorted and the 14 which indicate the greatest frequency of occurrence appear on a third printout, thus providing a list of the 14 movements having the relatively largest number of occurrences in the relatively fewest number of measures for each device in each of the possibilities (total, two-, three-, and four-voice texture). While it is not possible to list all statistical details here, illustrations of some of the information which has resulted from the study are included.

One of the first items of interest is the rank order and total number of occurrences of the selected nine devices. These appear in Table 1.

**TABLE 1

TOTAL, RATIOS, AND PROTOTYPICAL DISTRIBUTION**

![Image 1: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl1.jpg)

The devices are listed in rank order, descending, from left to right, first for the three-voice sections, and then for the four-voice movements. The number of occurrences of each device is given, including a breakdown showing two-voice and three-voice usage in the three-voice sections, and two-, three-, and four-voice usage for the four-voice movements. It is probably no surprise that the 4-3 suspension ranks first, or that the 2-1 suspension ranks last, but the list of the remaining devices should be of interest, both for the order and the amounts as well as for the fact that with only the exception of the 2-3 suspension, the order stays the same for the use of devices in the three-voice sections and the use in four-voice movements. (The dotted line in the middle of the table calls attention to the shift in order for the 2-3 suspension). Notice also that the breakdown into subgroups according to the number of voices sounding (at the point the device occurs) provides interesting information. Other than what is obvious for the harmonic 6/5, no occurrences were found of the consonant fourth or the 2-1 suspension in two voices, and only two 9-8 suspensions were found in two voices, one in the three-voice sections and one in the four-voice movements. (Since there was only the one in the four-voice movements, it is not included in the information available on the computer printout, and the entry appears in parentheses on the table.) While the 2-3 is third in rank order for the total number of occurrences in three-voice texture, it has the highest number of two-voice occurrences—far more than the 7-6, for instance. However, in the four-voice movements, the two-voice occurrences of the 7-6 outnumber those of the 2-3 by 156 to 148. In the four-voice movements there are more 7-6's, harmonic 6/5's, 2-3's, and 2-1's in three voices than in four.

Also included in Table 1 is the ratio of the number of occurrences of each device to the total number of bars, rounded to whole numbers. In the three-voice study, for instance, the 4-3 suspension occurs on an average of once every five bars, the 7-6 once every 15 bars, etc., while in the four-voice study, the 4-3 occurs once every four bars, the 7-6 once every ten bars, etc. These ratios serve as the basis for comparisons, and as the basis for arriving at the prototypical distribution which is also shown. In the three-voice sections, for example, for the average length of a section, which is 40 bars, the averaged or prototypical distribution is eight 4-3 suspensions, three 7-6 suspensions, two 2-3 suspensions, two accented passing tones, two _nota cambiata_ figures, one harmonic 6/5, and no 9-8's, consonant fourths, or 2-1's. The information in the last column to the right shows the ratio of the total number of devices to the number of measures; in three-voice sections it is 1:2.25, in four-voice movements it is 1:1.96, indicating that the devices occur slightly more frequently in the four-voice movements than in the three-voice sections. Further discussion of the information on Table 1 will not be undertaken at this point, but the reader is encouraged to glean information from the Table as appropriate to meet needs and satisfy curiosity.

Examination of all the data recorded produced little information which could serve as the basis for suggesting tendencies or trends regarding the use of the nine devices. For instance, attention was given to changes that might occur, in some methodical pattern, throughout the compositional period. With one exception no such pattern emerged. The exception is that in the four-voice movements, 291 of the 593 _nota cambiata_ figures occur in the first seven four-voice Masses (from volumes one and four of the Fratelli Scalera complete edition) and the remainder are distributed among the other 33 Masses, thus reflecting a marked decline in the employment of the _cambiata_. In the three-voice study, one tabulation grouped the entries according to the two most common voice combinations: cantus-altus-tenor and altus-tenor-bassus. The resulting ratios are quite similar to the ratios of the complete totals and there are only two instances of a change in rank order: in the cantus-altus-tenor arrangement, there are a few more _nota cambiata_ figures than accented passing notes, and in the altus-tenor-bassus voicing there are two more 9-8 suspensions, than harmonic 6/5 combinations. Differentiation by text setting was also examined. In the three-voice study, separate totals were tabulated for the _Crucifixus_, the _Pleni sunt coeli_ and the _Benedictus_ settings. Again, with only a few instances of a slight shift in rank position, the resulting ratios are very similar to those for the totals. Totals for the four-voice study were computed by movement (all the _Kyrie_ movements, all the _Credo_ movements, etc.). These results appear in Table 2.

**TABLE 2

COMPARISON OF TOTALS OF ALL MOVEMENTS TO TOTALS BY TYPE OF MOVEMENT**

![Image 2: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl2.jpg)

Most ratios for the movements are quite similar to those for the total of all movements. The rank order changes are indicated by the encircling of an entry whose raw score is higher than that of the entry to its left. On the basis of the ratios appearing in the right hand "Totals" column, the generality can be made that there is a slightly greater frequency of the devices in the shorter movements (_Kyrie_, _Benedictus_, _Agnus Dei_) than there is in the longer movements (_Gloria_ and _Credo_), but the differences do not seem terribly significant.

Besides the numbers of occurrences of the devices, special conditions sometimes attendant to each respective device were recorded. Included in the four-voice study for example are instances such as 104 suspensions in which the resolution note is already present in an accompanying voice, 851 4-3 suspensions accompanied by the melodic 6-5, 26 9-8 suspensions in which the ninth is a minor ninth and not a major ninth, various harmonic combinations with the 2-3 suspension, 63 accented passing tones approached by parallel dissonance or by leap to a dissonance, aspects of the preparation and resolution of the 6/5 harmonic combination, and 36 consonant fourths preceded by the harmonic 6/5.

Also listed were instances of the use of double nonharmonic devices. In the basic tally, each part of a double nonharmonic device was counted individually (for instance, a 9-8/4-3 double suspension was tallied as one 9-8 and one 4-3); therefore it was necessary to keep separate information regarding all such occurrences. Results of this tabulation appear on Table 3.

**TABLE 3 

DOUBLE NON-HARMONIC DEVICES**

![Image 3: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl3.jpg)

Notice that the double suspensions are subdivided into specific combinations, that there are more double suspensions than double _nota cambiata_ figures or double accented passing tones, and that there are many more double suspensions in four-voice movements than in three, with a correspondingly greater frequency of occurrence. Obviously it is necessary to subtract the number of suspensions involved in combinations from the totals which appear in Table 2 to get the number of _single_ suspensions. For example, there are 193 4-3 suspensions in a double-suspension combination; therefore, of the total 4,681 4-3 suspensions, 4,488 are single suspensions.

Another item of interest is the number of _different_ devices in any one movement. Table 4 shows graphically the percentage of the number of movements with the respective number of different devices.

**TABLE 4 

PERCENTAGE OF NUMBER OF MOVEMENTS WITH 

RESPECTIVE NUMBER OF DIFFERENT DEVICES**

![Image 4: vol23id233](http://symposium.music.org/SupportingFiles/ArticlesVol23No1/Hanson/HansonTbl4.jpg)

For instance, the three-voice sections, only one, or one percent, has just two different devices; nine sections, or twelve percent have three different devices; thirteen, or eighteen percent have four different devices, etc. The largest percentage (i.e., 29 percent) of the three-voice sections contains just five different devices, and only one has all nine devices. (Frankly, for pedagogical purposes, I was hoping to find a few more with all nine.) In the four-voice movements, graphed at the bottom of Table 4, notice that the distribution among movements with five, six, seven, and eight different devices is quite evenly balanced, and that there are eighteen movements, or nine percent of the total, that have all nine devices.

Of the previously-mentioned five purposes which the results of the study could serve, the first is to provide sources with many occurrences of each respective device. Specific references from the three-voice sections are in Table 5, and references from the four-voice movements are in Table 6.

EACH RESPECTIVE DEVICE**

The distribution of dissonance within most of the 19 examples does not come very close to the prototypical distribution, but of the 19 examples, 9 are three-voice sections from the Palestrinian Masses, and two of these are included on Table 7 as examples which approximate the prototypical distributions. One is the _Benedictus_ from the Mass _Gabriel archangelus_ and it is found in two books, in the collection of Soderlund[6](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x6) and in the text by Benjamin.[7](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x7) The other selection is the _Benedictus_ from the Mass _Repleatur os meum laude_. This is also found in the Soderlund collection,[8](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x8) and is included as well in the AtKisson text.[9](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#x9) The intent regarding this fourth purpose is not to suggest that selections in texts and anthologies are, are not, or should be based on the distribution of dissonance, but rather it is to suggest that it may often be in order for a teacher to call to the attention of students that certain aspects of a composition may contain some elements (or have omissions) which are not necessarily representative of a larger corpus of works, and in the case of Palestrina Mass movements, the information gathered enables one to be more specific concerning the kinds and amounts of nonharmonic devices which are encountered.

The fifth and last purpose is to accumulate a list of sources that illustrate devices used so seldom that they are considered rare or exceptional. While it is not the purpose of this report to give detailed information regarding these cases, the types of items include 4-5 or 7-8 lower-voice suspensions, the suspended diminished fifth, augmented triads in 6/3 position, diminished triads in 5/3 position (which are on a weak beat, and do not follow a 6/5), four eighth notes in a row, quarter note tones, high-note law exceptions, use of the Landini sixth melodic pattern, leaps to and/or from a dissonance, an upper neighbor tone in a half-note value, and syllable change with quarter notes.

A brief idea of the analytical study undertaken has been presented, along with some examples of specific resource information. Admittedly, further work is possible, including the enumeration of devices in five-voice (and more) Masses, in works other than Masses, and in works of other composers of the period, in both sacred and secular categories. But what has been done should help to substantiate the premise that the process of enumeration can play an important role in the ultimate product of illumination.

[2](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina#2)Herbert Kennedy Andrews, _An Introduction to the Technique of Palestrina_ (London: Novello and Company, 1958), p. 117.

(New York: Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1946), p. 166.

Lyrics

Poetic Translation

Sicut cervus desiderat ad fontes aquarum,

As the deer thirsts and pants for flowing fountains of water,

ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus.

That's how my soul desires, thirsting and panting for you, Father.

Sitivit anima mea ad Deum fontem vivum,

Thus thirsting, yearning is my soul for God the strong and living:

quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei?

When will I arrive to meet him and see the features of my Father?

Fuerunt mihi lacrymae meae panes die ac nocte,

They can't sustain me, tears that I scatter, bread for me day and nighttime,

dum dicitur mihi quotidie:

While every day, laughing, they say to me:

Ubi est Deus tuus?

Where is the God you long for?

Vulgate, Psalm 42

Carol Anne Perry Lagemann

# 09298215.2021.1877729

a In this paper, movements are defined according to the segmentation in the corpus ‘as found.’ Refer to Table for a simple tally of movements by number of parts. Note that in John Miller's dissertation he evaluates these proportions by ‘section’, where sectional boundaries are defined by changes in texture and metre, resulting in the following comparable distribution of part size to proportion (8: 3.5, 7: 0.3, 6: 15.7, 5: 34.6, 4: 36.6, 3: 5.4).

b The remaining 1.12% of slices have either all parts resting or only contain a single voice.

1 Notice that this is _not_ claiming that practice ought to _follow_ theory, but rather that we would expect practice to be _consistent_ with theory and vice-versa.

2 _Contrapuntal_ refers to a set of two or more voices singing independent melody lines at the same time. The harmonic interval they make when singing together is the _vertical_ or _harmonic_ interval. _Perfect consonances_ here refer to harmonic intervals forming a perfect fifth, fourth*, or perfect octave, or their compound equivalents (e.g. twelfth). *See also footnote 6.

3 For example: ‘Consecutive “octaves” by contrary movement … are rarely found in Palestrina's polyphony for fewer than five voices’ (p. 65). And, ‘In eight-part work, especially for double choir, strings of contrary movement consecutives are often found between the two bass parts as well as between other parts’ (Andrews, pp. 65–66).

4 It has been claimed that Palestrina's writing embodies the principles of counterpoint as taught by Zarlino (DeFord, [Citation 2015](https://doi.org/10.1080/09298215.2021.1877729#), p. 375).

5 Since Vicentino clearly uses ‘leap’ (Italian: _salti_) to refer to any melodic motion of a minor third or greater, I adopt the same definition.

6 Although harmonic perfect fourths are generally considered a dissonance in the Renaissance, Vicentino does include them in a few examples, and, in particular, they make a sizable subset of the rules for six-or-more voices. As such, rules with motion into perfect fourths are included here, though they are rare (4 rules in total move to P4).

7 While several additional rules can be found in book II meeting the above-described criteria, I excluded redundant rules, rules simply deemed ‘dubious’, and rules with conflicting labels.

8 This was done at Ohio State University in 2004 as per the README file in the corpus. To my knowledge there is no public published version of this corpus available online.

9 Although music21 contains a builit-in Palestrina corpus, it does not appear to be based on the corrected kern version and contains a different total number of movements. For more on Humdrum format see Huron ([Citation 1995](https://doi.org/10.1080/09298215.2021.1877729#)).

10 John Miller, in his dissertation, claims to have subdivided the standard movements of the mass by means of textural or metric changes and created a separate file for each, leading to a total of 1,327 files. However, the existing formats of this corpus are not divided in this way. As such, I label the movements based on the existing segregation of the files in the corpus, which typically ignores these textural changes in favor of having a consistent set of files that match the typical set of movements in the Mass Ordinary.

11 While typically only three intervals are needed to construct the fourth, as will be discussed, in this corpus compound intervals were collapsed, which required the full four intervals to be calculated.

12 A crude definition of _Musica Ficta_ is a term applied to all unnotated ‘inflections’ (raising or lowering of the pitch) that must be inferred from the musical context and was traditionally added by the performers themselves but in this case added by the editor of the original notated volumes. See Miller ([Citation 1992](https://doi.org/10.1080/09298215.2021.1877729#)).

13 I am referring to the specific examples used in this study. Elsewhere in _AMAMP_, Vicentino does reference specific parts (e.g. Book II, Chapter 18: ‘the minor sixth composed in various ways for two tenors’), and in these cases they typically contain more contextual detail, including specific rhythmic values and elaboration.

# Research: Phase 10.2 Preset 02 “Modal Linework” — Role A historical and primary-source report

**Reference:** Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina  
**Research role:** artist/style historian and primary-source researcher  
**Retrieval date for all web sources:** 21 February 2026  
**Method boundary:** this report uses abstract descriptions only. It does not reproduce melody. Publication dates are not silently treated as composition dates.

## Summary judgment

The most honest referential slice is **Palestrina’s mature, four-voice Latin sacred writing represented principally by the 1584 *Motettorum quatuor vocibus liber secundus*, especially the two-part *Sicut cervus / Sitivit anima mea*, with the four-voice *Missa Aeterna Christi munera* (published 1590) as a corroborating late mass source**. This corpus supports “four smooth modal voices with controlled dissonance” if the phrase means four singable, rhythmically differentiated lines organized through imitation, cadential articulation, and carefully situated passing/neighbor tones and prepared suspensions.

It must **not** imply four continuously sounding parts, a fixed modern church-mode scale, chord-pad voice leading, uniformly stepwise motion, blanket avoidance of dissonance, strict species-counterpoint exercises, equal thematic activity at every instant, guaranteed text intelligibility, or a simulation of Palestrina’s entire career. “Late” here securely describes **publication chronology** (1584–90), not necessarily the unknown dates when every constituent work was composed.

## 1. Scope and corpus

### Selected period and primary corpus

1. **Primary reference: *Motettorum quatuor vocibus liber secundus* (Venice, 1584), especially *Sicut cervus desiderat* and its secunda pars *Sitivit anima mea*.** The collection is explicitly for four voices; the bibliographic record identifies the 1584 print, while the surviving 1588 partbooks give direct near-contemporary witnesses. *Sicut cervus* is listed in the collection and the surviving facsimile locations identify Cantus, Tenor, and Bassus pages. [Collection record and facsimile links](https://stcpress.org/books/palestrina_motettorum_quartet_vocibus_liber_secundus); [work record](https://stcpress.org/pieces/sicut_cervus). **Confidence: high** for print, scoring, and witness; **medium** for calling the music itself “late-composed.”
2. **Corroborating late source: *Missa Aeterna Christi munera*, four voices, first printed as no. 1 of *Missarum liber quintus* (Rome: Francesco Coattino, 1590).** The Portuguese Early Music Database records the 1590 source and its witnesses/complete-edition concordances. [PEM database record](https://pemdatabase.eu/musical-item/66508); [1590 volume record](https://imslp.org/wiki/Missarum_-_Liber_Quintus_(Palestrina,_Giovanni_Pierluigi_da)). **Confidence: high** for publication and scoring.
3. **Comparative earlier source: *Motecta festorum totius anni*, liber primus (Rome, 1563/64), four voices.** This is included only to test persistence, not to redefine the preset around early work. Oxford’s institutional catalogue describes a scored-up copy of Palestrina’s 1563 first book; Schubert’s score-based study analyzes how its points of imitation are constructed. [Oxford MARCO catalogue](https://marco.ox.ac.uk/ark:29072/x0ff365497tf); Peter N. Schubert, “Hidden Forms in Palestrina’s First Book of Four-Voice Motets,” *JAMS* 60/3 (2007), 483–556, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2007.60.3.483). **Confidence: high**.
4. **Broad control corpus for dissonance claims: Palestrina’s four-voice masses.** Hanson counted 210 four-voice movements (18,313 bars) in 40 four-voice masses. Anders and Inden independently analyzed the first 36 Agnus movements in a machine-readable mass corpus, while explicitly documenting methodological limitations. These broader corpora prevent one celebrated motet from being mistaken for all practice. [Hanson 1983](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina); [Anders and Inden 2019](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244). **Confidence: high** for the reported corpus results; **medium** when transferred from masses to the selected motet.

### Score locations and audit points

- In the modern, source-linked St Cecilia Press score of *Sicut cervus*, audit **mm. 1–15** for staggered opening entries and changing voice count; **mm. 16–30** for continuation in overlapping lines; and **mm. 36–end** for renewed text/imitative activity and cadential convergence. The work page links these measures to a 1584 collection record and 1588 partbook images (Cantus/Tenor/Bassus at page 17 in the cited witness). [Score and facsimiles](https://stcpress.org/pieces/sicut_cervus). These measure numbers belong to the modern edition, not the unbarred partbooks. **Confidence: high** that these are appropriate audit spans; **medium** for any editorial barring-dependent boundary.
- For the mass, cite movement as well as measure because modern barring differs among editions: *Missa Aeterna Christi munera*, **Kyrie I opening through first cadence; Gloria opening declamation; Agnus Dei I opening and final cadence**. The stable primary identifier is *Missarum liber quintus* (Rome, 1590), no. 1. **Confidence: high** for source identity; **gap:** no single critical-edition measure concordance was available openly enough to privilege over movement/phrase locations.

### Exclusions

- *Missa Papae Marcelli* is not the central model: it is principally a six-voice work and would compromise the four-part claim.
- Five-voice Song of Songs motets and larger polychoral works are relevant to Palestrina’s range but excluded from the four-voice slice.
- Fuxian species exercises are reception history, not primary evidence of Palestrina’s compositional process.

## 2. Historical and aesthetic context

Palestrina worked in the institutional world of Roman Catholic chapels and published sacred music for a competitive print and patronage market. The selected works engage a mature sixteenth-century tradition in which independent vocal lines, points of imitation, cadences, text segmentation, and controlled mixtures of consonance and dissonance provide musical continuity and liturgical decorum. His idiom is not an isolated invention: imitation, paired entries, modal/tonal-type organization, cadential formulas, and regulated dissonance belonged to a shared Franco-Flemish/Italian contrapuntal vocabulary.

The Counter-Reformation matters, but the simple “Council of Trent demanded Palestrina’s style” narrative does not. Craig Monson’s document-based reassessment finds that the Council officially said little: it rejected profane/impure elements and left detailed regulation largely to local authorities. Therefore post-Tridentine concerns about sacred decorum and words are context, not a mechanical compositional specification. Craig A. Monson, “The Council of Trent Revisited,” *Journal of the American Musicological Society* 55/1 (2002), 1–37, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2002.55.1.1). **Confidence: high**.

The 1584 four-voice book also belongs to an unusually productive publication year: Palestrina issued three motet books that year, including this four-voice second book and two five-voice collections. Noel O’Regan’s print study supplies that publication context. Noel O’Regan, “Palestrina’s final motet print: the *Motettorum Quinque vocibus Liber Quintus* of 1584” (2023), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.25366/2023.146). **Confidence: high** for publishing context.

## 3. Career and style evolution

A neat early/middle/late ladder is less secure than reception literature often suggests, because print date, composition date, revision, and retrospective publication do not always coincide. The following bounded account is defensible:

1. **Early/public emergence (1550s–early 1560s):** first mass publication and Roman career established Palestrina in the international sacred-print repertory; the first four-voice motet book (1563/64) already exhibits sophisticated organization of imitative entries. Schubert shows that apparently unpredictable thematic-entry patterns in that book have intelligible contrapuntal/formal designs rather than mere continuous repetition. **Confidence: high** for the 1563/64 book and analyzed craft; **medium** for treating it as a unified “early style.”
2. **Middle publication phase (late 1560s–1570s):** Palestrina published mass and motet books in varied scorings and served multiple Roman institutions. The music cannot be reduced to one texture or one reform agenda. Hanson’s chronological observation supplies one concrete evolutionary finding: nearly half of the 593 *nota cambiata* figures found across 40 four-voice masses occur in the first seven masses of the edition’s ordering, with markedly fewer across the remaining 33. Hanson found no comparable systematic chronological trend among the other eight dissonance devices counted. **Confidence: medium** because edition order is an imperfect chronology, but the decline is evidence-based.
3. **Late publication phase selected here (1584–90):** the 1584 four-voice motet book and 1590 four-voice mass demonstrate continued investment in compact four-part sacred textures alongside five- and larger-voice repertories. The selected works retain imitation, text-responsive pacing, temporary thinning, and cadential convergence. **Confidence: high** for persistence in the scores; **medium** for claiming a distinctive, homogeneous late style.
4. **Very late breadth (to 1594):** Palestrina continued publishing in several sacred and spiritual genres. This breadth warns against making the selected four-part texture a whole-career essence. **Confidence: high**.

**Preset period decision:** reference **mature/late-published four-voice sacred polyphony, 1584–90**, centered on the 1584 motet book. Do not advertise “Palestrina’s late style” without the qualifier “late-published.”

## 4. Persistent traits versus period-specific traits

### Persistent or broadly recurring traits

- **Independent, singable lines coordinated contrapuntally.** “Smooth” is warranted as a contour-level tendency: steps predominate around carefully balanced leaps, and rhythmic overlap avoids four-part block motion as the default. It does not mean every interval is a step. **Confidence: high**, from selected scores and broader scholarship.
- **Imitation as articulated points, not an endless strict canon.** Entries may occur in changing orders and densities; Schubert’s first-book study identifies planned presentation types and formal intensification/relaxation. **Confidence: high** for the early book; **medium-high** as a persistent descriptor of the selected motet.
- **Texture breathes.** Four-voice scoring names the available parts, not a requirement that all four sound continuously. Voice rests, delayed entries, paired/partial textures, and convergence shape phrases. **Confidence: high** from scores.
- **Cadences are contrapuntal events.** Local two-voice cadential motions coordinate with continuing or arriving parts and segment text/form; they are not simply modern dominant–tonic chord changes. **Confidence: high**.
- **Dissonance is present and categorized by rhythmic and melodic context.** Weak-position stepwise passing and neighboring tones differ from accented prepared suspensions. Anders and Inden’s 36-Agnus corpus found large clusters of ascending/descending weak-beat passing tones, lower neighbors, and suspensions on strong beats 1 and 3. **Confidence: high** for that mass corpus; **medium-high** for the bounded preset inference.

### Period-/corpus-specific or unsafe to universalize

- **Exactly four voices** is specific to the chosen books/works; Palestrina frequently wrote five, six, and more parts. **Confidence: high**.
- **The affect and text pacing of *Sicut cervus*** belong to that psalm setting and should not become a universal serene/flowing affect label. **Confidence: high**.
- **Reduced use of *nota cambiata*** may characterize later portions of Hanson’s four-voice-mass ordering, but it is not proof of a wholesale late-style simplification. **Confidence: medium**.
- **Any single “mode” or final** is work-specific. Renaissance modal attribution involves final, range, signature/tonal type, cadence, and counterpoint; it is not a fixed pitch-class filter. **Confidence: high** in principle; **gap:** no single modal label is prescribed for the preset by this historical report.
- **Uniform text intelligibility** varies by passage, genre, acoustics, and performance. Imitative polyphony can clarify phrase boundaries yet blur simultaneous syllables. **Confidence: high**.

## 5. Relationship to peers and shared Renaissance vocabulary

- **Shared vocabulary:** imitation, contrapuntal modules, cadential formulas, regulated imperfect/perfect consonance, suspensions, passing tones, voice-pair textures, text-conditioned pacing, and modal/tonal-type organization are period practices, not Palestrina trademarks. Zarlino’s *Le istitutioni harmoniche* (Venice, 1558), part III, documents contemporary contrapuntal categories and treatment; the Utrecht *Thesaurus Musicarum Italicarum* supplies a critical digital text. [TMI critical edition](https://tmiweb.science.uu.nl/text/critical-edition/zarins58.html). **Confidence: high** for shared vocabulary; **medium** for any direct claim that Palestrina composed “from Zarlino’s rules.”
- **Lassus comparison:** Schubert and Lessoil-Daelman’s score-based comparison of related Kyries finds different uses of shared modeled material: Palestrina increases contrapuntal density “from within,” while Lassus builds longer formally structured spans. This supports a characteristic Palestrinian interest in saturating a texture through recombined contrapuntal relations, without declaring that technique unique. Peter Schubert and Marcelle Lessoil-Daelman, “What Modular Analysis Can Tell Us about Musical Modeling in the Renaissance,” *Music Theory Online* 19/1 (2013), especially paras. 22ff., [stable article](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.13.19.1/mto.13.19.1.schubert_lessoil-daelman.html). **Confidence: medium-high**; it is a case study, not a whole-career census.
- **Victoria comparison:** documented analytical work finds Victoria knew and reworked Palestrina, especially around Victoria’s 1572 collection. This demonstrates circulation and modeling, while Victoria’s own tonal/textual designs remain distinct. Daniele V. Filippi, “Formal design and sonic architecture in the motet around 1570: Palestrina and Victoria” (score-based study; bibliographic landing page), [record](https://www.academia.edu/4079888/Formal_design_and_sonic_architecture_in_the_motet_around_1570_Palestrina_and_Victoria). **Confidence: medium** because the accessible landing page/abstract, not a stable publisher full text, was available in this pass.

## 6. Unusually characteristic choices

These are useful differentiators only when phrased comparatively, not as exclusive inventions:

1. **Density through flexible ordering of imitative entries.** Schubert’s analysis of the first four-voice motet book shows why the number/order of subject entries can create concealed formal shapes and controlled heightening/relaxation. The result is neither random entrances nor mechanical four-entry fugato. **Confidence: high** for the analyzed book; **medium-high** for transfer to the selected late motet.
2. **Contrapuntal recombination that preserves line independence while increasing thematic saturation.** The Lassus/Palestrina case study identifies Palestrina’s tendency to densify a borrowed module internally. **Confidence: medium-high**.
3. **A high frequency but strong hierarchy of conventional dissonances.** Hanson’s four-voice mass census found 4–3 suspensions far more often than other counted devices (on average about one per four bars), with 7–6 suspensions about once per ten bars; double suspensions exist but are much less common than single ones. This is “controlled” because placement/preparation/resolution are constrained, not because tension is scarce. **Confidence: high** for Hanson’s corpus.
4. **Exceptions exist and matter.** Hanson documents rare leaps to/from dissonance, unusual suspended intervals, upper neighbors in longer values, and other exceptions. An honest model should treat textbook norms as weighted constraints, not historical absolutes—though an initial preset may reasonably omit rare exceptions and state that approximation. **Confidence: high**.

## 7. Common caricatures and myths to reject

1. **“Palestrina saved polyphony at Trent with the *Missa Papae Marcelli*.” — Reject.** Monson’s documentary study dismantles the simple causal story; the Council neither staged that canonical rescue nor issued a Palestrina rulebook. **Confidence: high**.
2. **“Palestrina style equals Fux’s five species.” — Reject.** Species counterpoint is later pedagogy and deliberately isolates textures/dissonance categories. Anders and Inden explicitly distinguish the five classroom categories from the additional categories and complexities in actual music. **Confidence: high**.
3. **“Controlled dissonance means almost no dissonance.” — Reject.** Hanson counts thousands of suspensions and hundreds of other accented devices in four-voice masses. Control concerns context and resolution. **Confidence: high**.
4. **“Four voices means four notes sounding at all times.” — Reject.** Entries, rests, and reduced textures are structurally important. **Confidence: high**.
5. **“Modal means choose Dorian and avoid chromatic notes.” — Reject.** Modal organization in Renaissance polyphony is not equivalent to a modern scalar preset; cadences, finals, range, signature, contrapuntal context, and editorial/performance *musica ficta* complicate the mapping. **Confidence: high**.
6. **“Smooth means no leaps, no accents, and no contrast.” — Reject.** Smoothness is aggregate line shaping; leaps are balanced, entries and suspensions create accents, and density changes articulate form. **Confidence: high**.
7. **“Every voice is equally thematic at every moment.” — Reject.** Imitative participation changes over time; some voices sustain, cadence, rest, or support while others state material. **Confidence: high**.
8. **“Palestrina is uniquely serene and impersonal.” — Reject.** This reception cliché overgeneralizes from selected works and performance traditions. Text, genre, scoring, and publication differ across his output. **Confidence: medium-high**.
9. **“All late Palestrina is simpler and more homophonic because of Trent.” — Reject.** The 1584 publications include sophisticated contrapuntal repertories in multiple scorings; Hanson found no broad chronological decline across most dissonance devices. **Confidence: high**.
10. **“A four-part algorithm can imitate Palestrina.” — Reject.** It can make a bounded arrangement approximation to selected relationships; it lacks Latin text-setting, source-specific modal plans, long-range imitative design, vocal rhetoric, and historically contingent performance practice unless those are explicitly modeled. **Confidence: high**.

## 8. Primary and authoritative evidence register

### Primary/near-primary sources kept

1. **Palestrina, *Motettorum quatuor vocibus liber secundus* (Venice, 1584); surviving 1588 partbook witness, Biblioteca de Catalunya digital collection.** Collection and folio/page links via [St Cecilia Press](https://stcpress.org/books/palestrina_motettorum_quartet_vocibus_liber_secundus); *Sicut cervus* facsimile locations and modern bar-numbered score via [work page](https://stcpress.org/pieces/sicut_cervus). Matters because it directly establishes the selected four-voice print and enables source/modern-score cross-checking.
2. **Palestrina, *Missarum liber quintus* (Rome: Francesco Coattino, 1590), no. 1, *Missa Aeterna Christi munera*.** [PEM institutional research database](https://pemdatabase.eu/musical-item/66508) and [volume scan record](https://imslp.org/wiki/Missarum_-_Liber_Quintus_(Palestrina,_Giovanni_Pierluigi_da)). Matters because it corroborates mature four-voice mass practice.
3. **Palestrina, first book of four-voice motets (Rome, 1563).** [Oxford Manuscripts and Archives catalogue](https://marco.ox.ac.uk/ark:29072/x0ff365497tf). Matters as a controlled earlier comparison.
4. **Gioseffo Zarlino, *Le istitutioni harmoniche* (Venice, 1558), part III, especially chapters on counterpoint, consonance/dissonance, and cadential motion.** [TMI critical digital edition](https://tmiweb.science.uu.nl/text/critical-edition/zarins58.html). Matters as contemporary theoretical evidence, not a claim of direct compositional obedience.

### Authoritative scholarship kept

5. **Peter N. Schubert, “Hidden Forms in Palestrina’s First Book of Four-Voice Motets,” *JAMS* 60/3 (2007), 483–556.** [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2007.60.3.483). Score-based account of points of imitation and formal shaping.
6. **Craig A. Monson, “The Council of Trent Revisited,” *JAMS* 55/1 (2002), 1–37.** [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2002.55.1.1). Document-based corrective to the Trent myth.
7. **Alice M. Hanson, “Enumeration of Dissonance in the Masses of Palestrina,” *College Music Symposium* 23 (1983).** [Full article](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina). Large score census with corpus totals, rates, exceptions, and explicit limits.
8. **Torsten Anders and Benjamin Inden, “Machine learning of symbolic compositional rules with genetic programming: dissonance treatment in Palestrina,” *PeerJ Computer Science* 5:e244 (2019).** [DOI/full text](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.244), esp. Fig. 1 (*Missa De Beata Maria Virgine* II, Agnus, mm. 24–26), Table 1, paras. 17–23, 32–54, 92–94. Reproducible corpus evidence for metric/melodic dissonance categories; authors disclose selection and detection limitations.
9. **Peter Schubert and Marcelle Lessoil-Daelman, “What Modular Analysis Can Tell Us about Musical Modeling in the Renaissance,” *Music Theory Online* 19/1 (2013).** [Article](https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.13.19.1/mto.13.19.1.schubert_lessoil-daelman.html). Score-based peer comparison.
10. **Noel O’Regan, “Palestrina’s final motet print…” (2023).** [DOI](https://doi.org/10.25366/2023.146). Publication-history context for the three 1584 motet books.

### Sources dropped or demoted

- **Wikipedia and generic composer biographies:** dropped as evidentiary authorities; useful only for orientation and unnecessary where institutional catalogues or scholarship exist.
- **Commercial recording notes and retailer descriptions:** dropped because aesthetic adjectives are not score-based evidence.
- **Emmanuel Music program note:** demoted; its description of gentle arches/word response is plausible but not needed to support the central claims.
- **CPDL user editions:** demoted to navigation/cross-checking; editorial provenance and barring vary. No claim rests solely on CPDL.
- **IMSLP metadata:** retained only as a scan/volume locator and checked against PEM or collection records; not treated as critical scholarship.
- **Academia.edu uploads:** the Filippi record is retained at medium confidence only for its bibliographic abstract; inaccessible/unstable full-text claims were not used.
- **Jeppesen and Fux as direct historical rules:** Jeppesen remains important reception/analysis and Fux important pedagogy, but neither substitutes for checking Palestrina’s scores; inaccessible book pages were not used for unsupported details.

## 9. Confidence, disagreements, and gaps

### Claim-level confidence summary

| Claim | Confidence | Basis / qualification |
|---|---|---|
| The 1584 second motet book and *Sicut cervus* are four-voice sacred sources | High | Print record and near-contemporary partbooks |
| *Missa Aeterna Christi munera* is four-voice and first printed in 1590 | High | PEM record and volume metadata |
| The selected slice supports smooth independent lines, imitation, cadential articulation, and contextual dissonance | High | Direct score plus multiple score/corpus studies |
| Weak-beat stepwise dissonances and prepared strong-beat suspensions are central categories | High for mass corpus; medium-high for preset generalization | Anders–Inden plus Hanson |
| Palestrina’s four-voice texture is not continuously four-part | High | Direct scores |
| Flexible entry order/density is unusually characteristic | High in first motet book; medium-high for selected late corpus | Schubert; direct audit supports transfer but no late-book census |
| The selected works constitute a homogeneous late compositional style | Low | Publication date does not prove composition date; therefore the report does not make this claim |
| Trent prescribed Palestrina’s style or the Marcellus Mass saved polyphony | High confidence false | Monson’s documentary reassessment |
| A single modern mode/scale captures the selected corpus | High confidence false | Historical modal organization and score evidence |
| Later masses use less *nota cambiata* | Medium | Hanson’s strong count but imperfect chronological ordering |

### Disagreements surfaced

1. **Textbook norm versus empirical practice:** Counterpoint manuals sometimes call devices typical/rare that Hanson’s census reverses (for example, relative frequencies of particular double suspensions). Use corpus frequencies over inherited textbook shorthand.
2. **Mode as work identity versus mode as analytic attribution:** Scholars disagree over how strongly traditional mode classifications explain polyphonic tonal organization. The preset may use a bounded modal pitch framework, but it must not present that mapping as a settled historical equivalence.
3. **“Palestrina style” versus Palestrina’s music:** Later pedagogy regularized selected features more strictly than the source repertory. The preset should say “Palestrina reference” and “bounded approximation,” not “authentic Palestrina counterpoint.”
4. **Late style versus late publication:** The evidence securely dates prints, not every composition. The selected label must remain “mature/late-published.”

### Residual gaps and next evidence steps

- No open critical edition with a stable measure concordance across *all* works in the 1584 four-voice book was verified. Before measure-level automated acceptance, choose one declared edition and create an incipit/text/measure concordance against the 1588 partbooks.
- The late four-voice motet book lacks the kind of complete entry-pattern census Schubert supplied for the first book. A score-by-score audit would be needed before claiming its entry ordering is statistically distinct from peers.
- Dissonance frequencies cited from Hanson and Anders–Inden are mass-based. They justify the general phrase but do not quantify *Sicut cervus* specifically. A transparent annotation of the selected 1584 motets would close that gap.
- *Musica ficta*, tuning, tactus, Latin prosody, and historical vocal deployment are intentionally not resolved here. They prevent “modal” from meaning a fixed MIDI scale but require separate specialist decisions.
- No inaccessible source has been replaced with a stronger unsupported claim. Where full text or critical pagination was unavailable, confidence was lowered or the claim omitted.

## 10. Decision for the parent synthesis

**Historian decision: conditionally support the catalog phrase.** The honest scope is:

> **A bounded arrangement reference to Palestrina’s mature, late-published four-voice sacred polyphony (principally the 1584 second book of four-voice motets, corroborated by the 1590 *Missa Aeterna Christi munera*): four singable modal-counterpoint lines whose imitative density and voice participation change through the phrase, with passing/neighbor dissonances in weak positions and prepared suspensions in accented positions, resolving within contrapuntal cadential motion.**

The short catalog phrase **“four smooth modal voices with controlled dissonance” is historically defensible only with that qualification**. It must not promise continuous SATB chordal filling, a single modern mode, mechanical species counterpoint, dissonance-free consonance, strict canon, automatic Latin-text rhetoric, or exact imitation of Palestrina.

## Sources

- **Kept:** 1584 *Motettorum quatuor vocibus liber secundus* / Biblioteca de Catalunya witness — direct selected source.
- **Kept:** 1590 *Missarum liber quintus* / PEM — corroborating four-voice mass source.
- **Kept:** Zarlino 1558 / TMI — contemporary theory and terminology.
- **Kept:** Schubert 2007; Monson 2002; Hanson 1983; Anders–Inden 2019; Schubert–Lessoil-Daelman 2013; O’Regan 2023 — peer-reviewed or scholarly score/document/corpus evidence.
- **Dropped/demoted:** Wikipedia, retailer and program notes, unstable user editions, and inaccessible secondary claims — insufficient authority or redundant.
